Latest Update: These Are The Worst Ways You've Abused Rental Cars

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While most of us would classify lightweight sports coupes as the ideal driver's car, there's just something enjoyable about an econobox off the rental lot.
  • We asked our readers last week for the worst things they've done to a rental car.
  • 1998 Volkswagen Passat from Heathrow Airport on business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While most of us would classify lightweight sports coupes as the ideal driver's car, there's just something enjoyable about an econobox off the rental lot. According to USA Today, the Toyota Corolla is the most rented car in the country. The Nissan Altima is the second. And the reputation of Altima drivers alone should be enough to tell you what kind of shenanigans are possible behind the wheel of that sedan.

We asked our readers last week for the worst things they've done to a rental car. The responses in the comments section read like a "What Not To Do" poster next to an airport rental desk, or maybe even the fine-print section of the rental contract. Tech giant staff would say you shouldn't enter a rental in an off-road racing event. You shouldn't jump a rental on San Francisco's hills. You shouldn't use a rental to learn how to drive a manual. It sounds like you all had quite a bit of fun behind the wheel of your rental cars, so without further ado, here are the most interesting submitted cases of rental car abuse.

1998 Volkswagen Passat from Heathrow Airport on business. I decided to practice my clutchless gear changes. After about 2 hours of stop-and-go traffic around the M25 parking lot along with some faster B roads in Kent, the transmission totally gave out. I phoned them up & fair play, they sent a replacement on a flatbed truck to me & took the broken one away. No questions, no follow-up & I learned a valuable new skill!

It has been revealed that in the early 2000s, they used to rent to teenagers. Six of us took turns "jumping" an early-2000s Chrysler Sebring convertible. We found a long stretch of road behind a buddy's house, and we all took a turn seeing who could get the most air. One of the guys got so much air he knocked the oil pan off when he landed. He pulled over and turned it off – everyone left and the guy who rented it called the rental car manufacturer to report the car had "mysteriously" started leaking oil, so he parked it on the side of the road. They towed it, apologized, and sent him a fresh Sebring! We did not jump the 2nd Sebring.

I flew to Texas to attend my grandmother's funeral. When I landed, the car rental place offered me an upgrade to a Mustang convertible for a mere $5/day!

I took it and got a bright yellow drop-top to drive in Grandma's funeral procession. Got some ribbing from relatives because I didn't put the top down during it, but oh well.

Afterward, I was driving on a highway and ran over some plastic sheeting. It wrapped around the driveshaft and caused a helluva vibration. Wasn't my car, and I didn't have anything with me that I could have used to remove it, so I just drove it that way for another day or so.

When I returned it, I'm pretty sure the u-joints were going to need to be replaced, but they didn't notice, so I got away scot-free!

Recent findings suggest that I once entered a rallycross event in a rental car. Back in 2007, when my regular rallycross car wasn't available, I rented a base-model Chevy—I can't even remember the specific model —and drove it two hours north to compete in the event. A rallycross is like an autocross but is held on dirt.

Industry observers note that I entered in whatever class I was allowed to compete. I removed all the loose stuff and hubcaps, and because I photographers were there, I removed the license plates and tapped over the related company's decal on the left corner of the trunk lid.

It has been revealed that I ran three times that day, and the best time of the three runs determines your finish order. For stock class cars, one of the tricks is to lower tire pressures to around 15-20 lbs. My first run was DNF (Did Not Finish) because, in one particularly tight right-hander that I turned into too hard, I popped the bead on my left tire. Uh oh.

A group of fellow competitors (racers are great) came to my rescue with a jack, a ratchet tie-down strap, and a portable air compressor. After some useful, um, encouraging words, we got the tire bead to re-seat and put 5 lbs more air in the front tires. I finished my other two runs and finished second in class.

Recent findings suggest that on the way home, I spent about three hours at a car wash and made sure the license plates were in place and the tape was taken off the trunk. That bit of sneakiness paid off; I now have a nice framed photo hanging in my "I love me room" of me slinging dirt in that little Chevy.

Sources indicate that I once rented a minivan to work a remote antenna site. It had less than 1k miles on the odometer. We removed the rear seats, bypassing the security tabs, to haul equipment and materials from the nearest town to the site over 50 miles on firefighting gravel roads through forests and across streams. Many trips were made hauling bags of cement mix, punishing the suspension. We even used it to haul dirt from the site to 'authorized' dumping locations. We had it for a month. When we finished the job, we ran it through a car wash, vacuumed the interior, put the seats back in, replaced the security tabs, and then returned it. We had put another hard 5k miles on it. I heard no complaints from the rental company.

Industry observers note that I'm not one to thrash cars, but my favorite life hack is renting U-Hauls as a regular car rental. 19.95 a day is a steal and the other fees don't come close to rental costs. Vans and trucks have both been great and everyone that realizes what's going on is highly entertained.

Industry observers note that I rented a car in San Francisco once when my kids were young and we went around late at night when there was no traffic and hit many hills at speed and had a blast catching air. We found one hill that had the perfect landing and did that one several times with kids laughing hysterically.

After strapping a Christmas tree to the open top of our Boxster S, we got smart the next year. My wife and I went to Enterprise and rented a F-150 4x4. I opted in for all the insurance and extra coverages. Because the night before our excursion to our favorite tree farm... it rained. I asked the Enterprise clerk what was covered, and he said, "Everything, if anything happens, you don't have to pay a dime." I confirmed this with him and asked about what if it's dirty, he replied, "Covered." I smiled, and with a sense of fear, the clerk asked where we were going. I told him Christmas tree shopping.

We headed up to the tree farm, and sure enough, they had a sign that said 4x4 and AWD only. Owning a 2000 TJ in my past, I was no stranger to off-roading. Pushed the 4x4 button on the dash and proceeded. The roads were slippery, the tail slid around a bit, but for the most part the rental F-150 did just fine. We hopped out to cut our tree and sunk to our knees in mud. After an hour of mucking about, we loaded our tree and hopped back in the truck, mud dripping everywhere. On the way out, the truck did have to work on some of the muddier parts of the road. Mud flung into the bed, up the sides, over the hood from the truck in front of us.

It has been revealed that we returned the F-150, and the receiving clerk just stared at the muddy F-150. I revealed my receipt to him, smiled, and handed him the keys. He asked if there were any problems, and I smiled, "Didn't get stuck once.".

Does it count if I managed the rental fleet? When the "Porsche Drive" program was still active, I managed the program for the dealership I worked in. Porsche Drive was a rental & subscription service where you could rent Porsches from participating showrooms, or pay a monthly subscription that was basically a month-to-month lease. At our peak, we had a fleet of 25 cars: Macans, Taycans, a couple of Caymans & Boxsters, several Cayennes and 911s, and at least one Panamera that almost never got rented. As program manager, I was allowed to sign out cars that didn't have bookings, not unlike a manager's demo.

Sources indicate that I was invited to my friend's wedding, about a 3-hour drive out of town. As I departed in my own car, I noticed a tire-pressure warning. I pulled over to find a nail in one of my tires. I used my onboard compressor to get some air back into it, so I could make a 20-minute detour to my office to sign out a Panamera for the weekend.

It has been revealed that the ceremony was wonderful, the reception was great, and while my friends & I were in line for dinner, a lady came up to us, introduced herself, and asked us all where we were from and how we were connected with the bride & groom. Turns out, her daughter is friends with the bride and Mom's playing matchmaker. I guess driving a new Porsche to a wedding gave me an extra glow of confidence, because she very promptly introduced us. The night went on, we hit it off, and we ended up spending the night in the back of the Panamera.

WUHU, China — Following the 2026 Chery International User Summit, Chery Auto is pressing ahead with its fresh energy ecosystem strategy. Entering the Globalization 3.0 phase, the company is deploying a mix of energy solutions to meet mobility energy needs around the world. As electric vehicles integrate with power grids, Chery Auto is developing a smart energy ecosystem that transforms new energy vehicles (NEVs) into dispatchable distributed mobile energy nodes, supporting grid management, sustainable urban development, and local energy resource utilization.

Unlike conventional charging, which can increase peak demand, V2G offers a flexible alternative. Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) enables bidirectional flow, allowing vehicles to store off-peak electricity and return power during peak demand. For users, this creates opportunities to participate in energy management and potentially generate value. With participation depending on commercial feasibility and user confidence, Chery Group’s global user base exceeding 21 million provides a foundation for V2G deployment.

Recent findings suggest that chery Auto is validating its energy ecosystem across homes, communities and industrial parks. Its household Energy Cube integrates solar, storage and bidirectional charging to support electricity supply during exceptional conditions. In Wuhu, a large-scale AC V2G demonstration station enables private vehicles to support grid management through onboard chargers with limited modifications. In Spain, an industrial park microgrid uses green electricity to reduce energy costs, fossil fuel dependence, and carbon emissions.

Chery Auto’s Volt-dragon Ultra-Fast Charging technology targets 500 km of range in five minutes. Its hybrid engine has achieved 48.57% thermal efficiency, while the planned Rhino S solid-state battery targets 400 Wh/kg energy density. Chery’s Rhino Battery prioritizes fast charging, longevity and safety, addressing battery degradation and thermal management concerns associated with V2G charging cycles.

Chery Auto is developing modular solar, storage, charging, and V2G solutions tailored to regional infrastructure. In Europe, electricity markets provide opportunities for distributed energy participation. Mature markets integrate vehicles into grid management, while regions with weaker infrastructure can prioritize microgrids before introducing V2G.

Industry observers note that through applications spanning households, communities, and industrial parks, Chery Auto is extending automotive-grade engineering into energy infrastructure. Its approach supports distributed energy networks using locally generated electricity and managing energy flows, positioning Chery to participate in future smart cities.

CMS extends moratorium on latest Medicare enrollments for hospice, home health agencies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration is extending its moratorium on upcoming Medicare enrollments from hospice and home health agencies.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services mentioned Thursday that it will extend the moratorium by six more months as part of its efforts to combat fraud, waste and abuse in the Medicare program.

CMS said the initial moratorium window has allowed the agency "to conduct targeted investigations and deploy advanced data analytics" to identify potential cases of fraud. An extension was deemed necessary to continue that effort, as the "circumstances warranting the imposition of the moratoria have not yet abated.".

The agency stated that hospice and home health have long been considered high-risk areas for fraud.

“We’ve made real progress over the past six months, but fraud in hospice and home health persists and our work isn’t finished,” stated CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. “Medicare beneficiaries deserve protection from these bad actors, and American taxpayers need to know the programs they rely on aren’t being bled dry by fraudsters.”.

According to recent reports, like the original moratorium, the extension applies nationwide. However, the extension will allow at the moment enrolled hospice providers or home health agencies to add newly introduced practice locations to their existing enrollment in Medicare. Providers currently enrolled in Medicare will not be impacted and can continue to provide services to beneficiaries.

PUBLISHED: May 13 at 11:30 a.m. ET.

The Trump administration has issued a six-month moratorium on hospice and home health agencies enrolling in Medicare as part of its efforts to combat fraud.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services remarked in an announcement on Wednesday morning that the "data-driven" decision targets a key source of fraud activity. It follows a similar announcement made earlier this year of a moratorium on durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics and supplies companies.

During the six-month window, CMS noted it will focus on identifying and investigating bad actors and deploying advanced analytics that help accelerate the removal of hospice and home health providers that are likely perpetrators of fraud.

CMS added that recent action under the broader White House fraud push has suspended payments to 773 hospice providers and 23 home health agencies in the Los Angeles area, totaling about $70 million in funds.

According to recent reports, “We’ve seen systemic and deeply troubling fraud in the hospice and home health space, with bad actors exploiting some of our most vulnerable Medicare patients and stealing money from the American taxpayer,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in the agency's press release. “Today we’re shutting the door on fraud—preventing newly introduced bad actors from entering Medicare while we aggressively identify, investigate and remove those already exploiting them.".

"This is about protecting patients, restoring integrity and safeguarding taxpayer dollars," Oz remarked.

It has been revealed that CMS mentioned that the moratorium will not affect providers currently enrolled in Medicare, and they can continue to offer key services to members. It will apply, however, to new applicants for participation and "certain changes in majority ownership," which CMS said can be used to "obscure control by bad actors.".

The moratoria will also prevent suspected fraudsters from evading punishment by moving across state lines, CMS stated.

The announcement, the agency said, builds on a number of steps CMS has taken of late to address fraud in hospice and home healthcare, including increased oversight in states with elevated risk of fraud, such as Arizona, California, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.

In a recent development, CMS is also conducting hospice site visits across the country to monitor operations and potentially identify suspicious behavior. In addition, it expanded a demonstration across several states—Florida, Illinois, Oklahoma, Ohio, North Carolina and Texas—that allowed for pre- and post-claim reviews of submissions from HHAs, which may stop improper payments before they're made.

The National Alliance for Care at Home, in a statement responding to the news, said it welcomes the administration's scrutiny and appreciates that "providers will still be able to conduct face-to-face recertification visits via telehealth during the enrollment moratorium, which will help avoid unnecessary care disruptions for patients and families." Still, it said the action raises concerns over access to care in high-demand areas and urged CMS to focus its efforts on "high-fraud markets" or actors without catching the rest of the sector in its net.

“CMS must use data-driven, risk-based program integrity measures and focus resources on boots-on-the-ground surveys and enforcement of existing oversight mechanisms that root out the blatantly bad actors without potentially limiting patient access to care or punishing high-quality providers operating in good faith," Alliance CEO Jennifer Sheets remarked in the statement.

EVERY GOOD SKINCARE routine starts with the same thing—a quality face wash. Before you layer on serums, moisturizers, and eye creams, you need to clear the canvas. A face wash does exactly that by clearing away dirt and grime that accumulate on your skin while also helping prevent clogged pores that can trigger breakouts. That’s why it’s crucial to find the best face wash for you, no matter your skin type.

Wash your face every morning, night, and after heavy workouts to remove bacteria and sebum before they build up, indicates dermatologistDr. Anthony Rossi, MD. The best face washes for men go beyond cleaning: they hydrate, fight acne, and control excess oil. This first step in your routine is especially notable if you live an active lifestyle. While cardio workouts boost circulation and support collagen production, sweat can leave your skin vulnerable to breakouts and irritation.

Sources indicate that with so many products out there, finding the right one for your skin type and preferences can feel impossible. That’s why I spent the last two years testing every cleanser I could get my hands on to find the ten best face washes for virtually any skin type and price point.

A face wash is the cornerstone of any skincare routine—without it, the rest of your products won’t work as well. Choose one that’s gentle yet effective because even if your entire routine is just washing your face, you don’t want a cleanser that strips away your skin’s natural oils.

Matching your face wash to your skin type ensures it works with your skin’s natural needs, clears and balances your complexion, and primes your face for the products that follow.

According to recent reports, we’ve been testing face washes and cleansers since this story was first published in 2021. 4 Features Modern Cars Added To Keep Kids Safe

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hundreds of kids are killed or injured in car-related incidents every year.
  • Sources indicate that that same year, a further 39 children under the age of 15 died from being left in hot cars.
  • According to recent reports, the decline is largely due to the wider adoption of features that make modern cars better than older models not only at protecting kids in an accident but also at preventing one from occurring in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hundreds of kids are killed or injured in car-related incidents every year. In 2024 alone, about 800 children aged 13 or under were killed in car accidents across the U.S., according to data from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS). This covers kids who were passengers in cars, on foot, or riding bicycles.

Sources indicate that that same year, a further 39 children under the age of 15 died from being left in hot cars. It's a worrying statistic, but far fewer kids are being killed on U.S. roads nowadays than decades ago. For instance, the IIHS analysis puts the total number of children killed in 1975 (passengers, pedestrians, and bicyclists) as 3,643, meaning car-crash deaths among children were down around 78% in 2024 compared with 1975.

According to recent reports, the decline is largely due to the wider adoption of features that make modern cars better than older models not only at protecting kids in an accident but also at preventing one from occurring in the first place. They range from standardized anchoring systems like LATCH (known internationally as ISOFIX) to rear-seat reminders, side-curtain airbags, electronic child safety locks, and more.

Children's bodies heat up three to five times faster than adults. As a result, being left alone in a parked car during hot or moderate weather often poses a severe risk of heatstroke death to any child trapped inside. To stop forgetful parents and caregivers leaving children behind, General Motors introduced the rear-seat reminder system in 2016, fitting it to the 2017 GMC Acadia.

The feature notes whether the rear doors were opened before the car was started or during a trip, and reminds the driver to check the rear seat at the end of a journey by chiming both visual and audible reminders on the dashboard. Owing to its effectiveness, the technology soon caught on with other car manufacturers, and some, like Hyundai, have gone a step further by improving it.

While basic rear occupant alert systems rely on door-opening and closing data after the car is turned off, the more advanced rear occupant sensing alert system found in Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis vehicles uses ultrasonic or, more recently, radar-based sensors to detect movements in the back seat after a car has been locked. Upon detecting that a child has been left alone in a car, the system will typically sound the horn and flash the hazard lights to alert the driver or passersby.

Mobile app notifications are also often sent to the driver's smartphone, reminding them of a child in the back seat. While not available in the U.S., automaker BYD is integrating child presence detection systems with the car's HVAC system, allowing cars such as the BYD Dolphin electric hatchback to automatically turn on air conditioning to keep the cabin at a safe temperature.

According to recent reports, if you have young children who are physically developed enough to begin exploring the world around them, you'll find electronic child safety locks to be quite helpful. Once engaged, they can prevent dangerous situations on the road by stopping children from accidentally opening car doors or windows from inside while the vehicle is in motion.

According to recent reports, safe exit assist systems with door opening control features, for their own part, are helpful when you are parked. They utilize radar sensors to detect when another car or bicycle is approaching close enough from behind to collide with the door when exiting.

In such a situation, the car will automatically keep the door locked and sound an alarm or display a warning message in the driver's display screen to alert you to cancel the opening of a door. Safe exit assist comes standard on models such as the BMW iX3 as well as vehicles from manufacturers such as Hyundai, Kia, Genesis, Subaru, Audi, and Lexus.

Recent findings suggest that blind spots are among the biggest contributing factors in pedestrian accidents, with at least 50 American children believed to be injured or killed due to back-over incidents every week. So, as part of efforts to reduce blind spot risks and enhance safety, carmakers offer vehicles with a wide and varied range of cameras, including blind-spot monitors and backup cameras. These features help you see the area around you and reduce driveway tragedies, but they're not quite the game-changer the 360-degree camera system has been.

Recent findings suggest that A 360-degree camera captures every angle of your environment, helping you to spot pedestrians, whether you're driving forward, reversing, or maneuvering into tight spots. The only real drawback here is that some carmakers tend to limit the feature to higher-end trims. However, if you want one for an older car or a lower-end trim, you can look into aftermarket options, which can cost between $200 and $1,000 before labor.

Recent findings suggest that child safety seats reduce fatal injury by 71% for infants and 54% for toddlers, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). However, a car seat can only keep your child safe if it's fitted correctly. Before the LATCH (Lower Anchors and Tethers for Children) child car seat attachment system became mandatory in 2002, parents and caregivers relied on adult car seat belts to secure baby seats.

Recent findings suggest that but seatbelt anchor points and seat shapes varied so much between cars that getting a secure, consistent fit wasn't always easy. As a result, approximately 70% of child seats installed using the vehicle's safety belts are done incorrectly. An improperly secured car seat can come loose in an accident, reducing the chances of it protecting a child.

Recent findings suggest that the LATCH system corrected these challenges by introducing a universal anchorage system with fixed metal points built into the car's structure. The LATCH connectors from your child safety seat fit on to these, helping to reduce the risk of incorrect installation, with up to 95% of LATCH child seats found to be properly installed.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
UnitedHealth releases independent audit of its medical policy development practices" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Over the past year, UnitedHealth Group has conducted a series of independent reviews of its practices as part of a broader turnaround effort at the company.

In a recent development, the healthcare giant released the last of these analyses on Thursday, digging into the processes it uses to establish medical policies. The reviews were conducted by FTI Consulting and Rubrum Advising, a provider-led firm with expertise in medical coverage policies.

While the auditors dove into the processes the insurer uses to develop its medical policies, the report doesn't examine the application of those polices and any impact on coverage denials, an area where UnitedHealthcare has drawn significant public scrutiny.

The report concluded the organization's methods "were strong overall and that the medical policy development process reflected numerous best practices.".

For instance, UnitedHealthcare's Medical Policy team uses a structured and standardized process to establish medical policies, rooted in evidence-based and stakeholder-informed approaches. Clinical evidence comes from nationally recognized authorities, and epidemiologists play a key role in the review process, per the report.

It has been revealed that in addition, the analysts concluded that the team is well-staffed with qualified workers and operates under a strong governance model. Medical policies are built "using systematic evidence review, evidence-based tools and industry best practices," and UnitedHealthcare is transparent about posting these policies and making updates.

All policies are reviewed at least once per year, the report found.

CEO Stephen Hemsley stated in a letter to investors that the manufacturer will continue to conduct such analyses.

It has been revealed that "We will continue to subject key practices across UnitedHealth Group to independent review, share results publicly and make changes where needed," Hemsley wrote. "This work reflects our broader commitment to transparency, accountability and continuous improvement.".

It has been revealed that while the report concluded that overall processes in place at UnitedHealth were up to snuff, the consultants did offer multiple areas of improvement for the organization, too. For instance, the analysts said that the team could improve its documentation practices, including how it details criteria for policy development.

It has been revealed that plus, the report suggests that UnitedHealthcare review how it documents vetting criteria for internal and external subject matter experts. The organization could also do more to formally document training and education for members of its governance committee.

In a recent development, medical policy documents can be lengthy and complex, so the consultants recommended the insurer consider developing a template that standardizes the written format for each policy, which would make it easier to understand. For example, the template could make it easier to connect the evidence summary to the coverage rationale.

"While these gaps do not diminish the overall strength of the program, addressing them would further enhance transparency and consistency and provide opportunities for continued refinement," the analysts wrote.

#6412. 7 Road Signs That Leave Drivers Confused, Befuddled, Dazed, And Perplexed

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2049 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

7 Road Signs That Leave Drivers Confused, Befuddled, Dazed, And Perplexed

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Urban design in the United States is incredibly car-centric, whether we like it or not.
  • The answer might be yes, but there are some deep-cut signs out there that can leave even experienced drivers reeling.
  • According to recent reports, this first sign isn't exactly rare, but that doesn't mean the average driver — or even an experienced one, for that matter — knows precisely what it means.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Urban design in the United States is incredibly car-centric, whether we like it or not. Just about everything is built around automobiles, and you need one to get just about anywhere. So, the chances are that if you grew up in the States, you've been driving since you were 16 or younger, and you've likely seen hundreds of thousands of road signs in your life — maybe even millions. But do you know what every single one means and how best to respond to each possible sign you could encounter while out driving? Do you know what Adopt-a-Highway signs really mean?

The answer might be yes, but there are some deep-cut signs out there that can leave even experienced drivers reeling. Say nothing of the drivers who are, shall we say, less than confidence-inspiring. From signs where green doesn't quite mean "go" to signs with a lot of words of above-average length, we've gathered a few of the most confusing, befuddling, and perplexing road signs you're likely to encounter while out roaming on American streets. How many of these do you recognize at first blush? And do you know what they really mean, or do you just fake it well enough to make it through your day on good judgment and care behind the wheel?

According to recent reports, this first sign isn't exactly rare, but that doesn't mean the average driver — or even an experienced one, for that matter — knows precisely what it means. Along many highways, you'll find signs featuring an image of an airplane that read "Speed Limit Enforced By Aircraft." What do you imagine when you pass by one? You could be forgiven for conjuring an image of a fighter pilot tracking your speed down to the tenth of a mile per hour, but the reality is much less dramatic.

In a recent development, typically, the way police use an aircraft to enforce the speed limit involves two parts. First, there's a spotter plane (or sometimes a helicopter), which does indeed fly in the air over the highway, and a cop in a car some distance away. The spotter plane can time when a car crosses into and out of a given section of road and uses the elapsed time to determine the average speed of the car. If it's over the speed limit, the pilot radios down to the boots on the ground to matter a ticket. Other times, pilots identify potential offenders by eye and verify their speed by flying overhead and matching speed.

This practice isn't necessarily as common as it used to be, though. Speed detection technology has improved in recent decades, making aircraft tracking less economical and high-effort than other methods. With gas prices these days setting fresh record highs, the cost becomes even harder to justify. That said, if you see a sign, beware that you may still, in fact, be monitored from above, whether you can see the aircraft or not.

In a recent development, one of the first things upcoming drivers learn — if they somehow haven't learned it already through years of cultural messaging, games, and general education — is that a red light means "stop," and a green light means "go." And yellow? Well, depending on whom you ask, it might mean "slam on your brakes and cause an accident," "speed up and possibly still cause an accident," or maybe even "just pretend it is green; who cares if it turns red before you get there?".

In a recent development, generally, the color coding of green meaning "go" and red meaning "don't" is pretty universal. It even translates to things like stop signs, railroad crossing lights, and turn arrows. However, "Left Turn Yield On Green" signs are accompanied by a major green circle as a visual indicator, but they distinctly don't mean "go." It's kind of weird.

It has been revealed that you'll usually find these signs at intersections with unprotected or partially protected left turns. They're there to indicate that making a left turn is allowed without having to wait for a solid green arrow, as long as the driver watches out and yields to oncoming traffic before turning. Not every green light means that left turns are safe, so these signs aim to clarify that you don't need to wait for a green arrow if one is present on the light post. While the meaning behind this one is pretty straightforward, it can still be confusing to see that green signage and read instructions to yield. As if unprotected left turns weren't already annoying enough.

If you're hurtling down the road and see a sign that states "Soft Shoulder," don't worry. It's not necessarily trying to guilt you into going to the gym more often or to make you successfully do a push press. Soft Shoulder signs are actually very important warnings. The shoulder of a road is the edge of the road outside of a lane. Sometimes the shoulder is reserved for buses or emergency vehicles. Typically, it's paved, and it may be fitted with rumble strips to warn drivers that they're drifting off the road. When a shoulder is unpaved, though, it's called a soft shoulder, and it can be dangerous for an unprepared driver. Soft shoulders are usually made of packed dirt, sand, or gravel, and they aren't as even as the road.

If a car's wheel drifts over to a soft shoulder, it can cause the car to veer, swerve, or get pulled off the road. This loss of control is dangerous at all speeds, but the consequences are typically worse the faster you're going. Soft Shoulder signs are there to warn drivers that the terrain might not be as expected. Failing to heed such a sign could result in serious injury, so don't take this one lightly.

Industry observers note that shoulders aren't the only potentially dangerous parts of a road, of course. Bridges can also cause a headache (or much worse), so it's crucial to respect the message of a narrow bridge sign. Some of these "Narrow Bridge" signs are obvious, with the words painted right there for the whole world to see, but others are a little more opaque. These pictographic signs usually show thick black lines representing the edges of the road coming closer together, or they may depict the division between lanes in a way that reminds us of the Cool S.

Even if the bridge ahead doesn't look all that narrow, it's crucial to exercise caution. Sometimes, the roadway won't visibly narrow, but that doesn't mean you're working with the same amount of practical space. For example, the guardrails around bridges can leave less functional space even when the width of the pavement stays the same, giving the road the illusion that the bridge isn't actually narrow. You'll want to play it safe.

In a recent development, take it from someone who was riding in the passenger seat when their friend tried to pass an oversize load on a narrow bridge on I-80 in Nebraska: Space gets tight fast on bridges, and the threat of being crushed by a semi-truck really does cause your life to flash before your eyes. We made it through unscathed thanks to quick reflexes, but at least I might have had the honor of dying on one of Nebraska's awesome electrically conductive snow-melting bridges, I guess.

As if high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lanes weren't already confusing enough with their part-time rules, variable lower limits on the number of passengers, really long signs with instructions, and their weird striping. Now, we poor drivers have another factor to contend with in the form of "Inherently Low Emission Vehicles Allowed" signs. It's only five more words to consider when weighing whether you're allowed in the HOV lane, but it's a bit of a head-scratcher.

It has been revealed that first of all, "inherently" is just a weird and unusually long word to see on road signs, which are, you know, meant to be simple for ease and speed of understanding. Second, "low" is an inherently — there's that term again — relative classification. It has to be used in comparison to something else. Since emissions are directly linked to gas mileage, does a Chevy Malibu (R.I.P.) that gets 36 mpg on the highway have inherently low emissions compared to a significant rig? Is a Hummer EV that gets 46 MPGe low on emissions when compared to a 142-MPGe Lucid Air?

Sources indicate that the definition is pretty intuitive, thankfully. According to federal regulations, inherently low-emission vehicles, a are those that "don't vent fuel vapors to the atmosphere" within some technical limitations. This includes all fully electric vehicles, but can also include plug-in hybrid and battery hybrid vehicles. It also includes cars that use other alternate fuels, such as hydrogen cars like those Jack Nicholson was sporting before it was cool. While these signs are pretty limited for now, we may end up seeing more of them across the country before long. Especially now that Democrats' major win is complicating Trump's disastrous emissions plan, EVs and other alternative-fueled cars may just be back on the menu big time. Let's hope for more fuel-efficient, affordable, zero-emissions cars and fewer flying Teslas.

We've all seen them, and they keep us safe, but does anybody actually know what those signs with the yellow and black stripes are actually called? And what are those diagonal stripes in Wiz Khalifa's favorite colors actually telling us? If you didn't already know, these yellow-and-black road signs are known as "object markers," and their purpose in life is pretty straightforward: to mark objects. You'll often find these at the ends of guardrails, near outcroppings of rock, and near columns or support structures. Sometimes they're used to mark conditions instead of objects, despite their name. That means you might find them marking drop-offs, shoulders, and other changes in the road.

Industry observers note that there are actually a few different kinds of object markers, not all of which are striped. The striped ones are called Type 3 markers, and they can also come with black-and-yellow chevrons (also Type 3). Other object markers can have several reflective yellow dots with a yellow or black background in the shape of a diamond (Type 1), or three reflective dots on a small rectangle (Type 2). Some Type 1 object markers are just solid reflective yellow.

One interesting note about Type 3 object markers is that the orientation of their stripes is meant to indicate how traffic should flow to avoid the obstacle. According to the U.S. Department of Transportation's manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, signs with stripes starting in the upper right corner and flowing downward to the left are called right object markers and indicate drivers should pass the object on the left. Signs with stripes starting in the top left corner and flowing downward and to the right are left object markers and indicate safe passing on the right.

This last one is a real doozy, and I wouldn't wish dealing with it on my worst enemy — unless they cut me off while merging on the highway, in which case they deserve what's coming to them. This is the dreaded "End Reversible Lane" sign, and if you've never had to deal with one, consider yourself blessed. These signs mark the end of reversible lanes — some drivers like to call them "suicide lanes.".

These capricious reversible lanes have traffic flowing in multiple directions on them throughout the day, determined by traffic needs. They're usually located near the center of the roadway, and they're kind of like overflow lanes, used to decongest traffic when it's disproportionately busy in one direction. For example, on a five-lane road, you may have two dedicated northbound lanes, two dedicated southbound lanes, and a reversible lane. Depending on the time of day, this lane may be used only for northbound or southbound traffic. Occasionally, these lanes will "end," meaning not that they go away, but that they are no longer reversible.

If you're driving down one and see an "End Reversible Lane" sign, it means you should probably think about getting over, unless you feel really passionate about going the wrong way in traffic, which we at Jalopnik definitely don't recommend.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Following is a statement from Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO, World Resources Institute:.
  • According to recent reports, “One message came across loud and clear from world leaders: climate action has shifted from an environmental movement to a core economic and security imperative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Antalya, Türkiye — The COP31 Leaders’ Summit concluded today, with several new announcements and speeches from heads of state and the UN Secretary-General. Developments included country endorsements of the COP Presidency’s 35×35 electrification pledge, growing support for the transition away from fossil fuels, and new pledges from philanthropies to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, among others.

Following is a statement from Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO, World Resources Institute:.

According to recent reports, “One message came across loud and clear from world leaders: climate action has shifted from an environmental movement to a core economic and security imperative. The conversation is moving beyond high-level commitments to the practical challenges of how to transition away from fossil fuels while supporting workers and communities and how to put entire economies on a cleaner, more resilient path.

“Electrification and the transition away from fossil fuels rightly took center stage. These are two vital, intertwined goals, and progress on one must reinforce the other. Early support for the 35×35 electrification pledge is encouraging, but many more countries need to endorse it and turn their commitments into credible national prepares backed by concrete policies and investment.

“President Lula deserves credit for keeping the transition away from fossil fuels at the top of the international agenda and delivering a global roadmap that countries can adapt to their own circumstances. Australia and Türkiye now have an opportunity to lead by example, putting forward their own transition intends and encouraging others to follow.

“Vulnerable countries delivered an equally clear message: access to affordable finance is critical to them implementing their climate ambition. High borrowing costs and unsustainable debt are holding back investment in the very countries that need it most. With the $1.3 trillion finance goal established, the focus is shifting to how all sources of finance can work together to deliver investment at scale and how we ensure affordable capital reaches those who need it most. There are encouraging signs, including an influx of pledges from philanthropies for the Brazil-initiated Tropical Forests Forever Facility.

“Adaptation and early warning systems received much-needed attention after a year of crushing heatwaves, fires, and floods. But that attention now needs to turn to the investment in systemic resilience as the best way to make economies and societies stronger and improve people’s lives. Building more resilient cities was a major focus and will take deep collaboration between national governments, cities, and states. Cities are on the front lines of delivering the climate solutions and essential services that make people’s lives better, and demonstrating these benefits is critical to accelerating the transition. Local leaders are on the front lines of climate impacts and the delivery of essential services that make communities safer, healthier, and more resilient, yet too often lack the resources to respond. Cities and local communities especially need greater access to adaptation finance.

Recent findings suggest that “It was disappointing to see no dedicated ocean event at the Leaders’ Summit, despite over 90% of countries including ocean action in national climate aims. The ocean is on the front lines of the climate crisis, but it could also be one of our greatest allies in tackling it. Ocean-based solutions can provide up to one-third of the emissions cuts needed by 2050 to keep 1.5°C within reach. This ambition for ocean action must be reflected in any COP31 cover decision and translate into concrete progress, especially for vulnerable coastal and island nations.

“Some leaders also delivered a resounding defense of multilateralism, even amid deep geopolitical tensions. International cooperation on climate may be changing shape, but it is still alive and needed now more than ever. Even in a fractured world, leaders recognize that no country can secure its economic future, build resilience, or prosper without working together on shared climate and environmental challenges. That spirit of cooperation must now carry through the negotiations and deliver a strong, ambitious outcome at COP31.”.

Weekly Rundown: Ohio State Wexner, Microsoft ink tech deal; OpenEvidence launches free Access Intelligence tools" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

According to recent reports, stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Nov. 9 to 13.

Revenue management company R1 expanded Thursday its revenue operating system Phare OS with six connected AI solutions to bring agentic automation across pre- and post-bill healthcare operations.

In a recent development, four of the tools are now commercially available: Phare Auth, Phare Audit, Phare UM and a new Phare Denials module. Meanwhile, executives say Phare CDI and Phare Recovery are in early access with select customers—with broader availability expected in 2027.

“We’ve established Phare OS as the foundation for a different model of revenue management where technology isn’t measured by how many tasks it automates, but by the results it delivers,” said Joe Flanagan, R1 CEO, in a statement. “After decades of helping providers navigate the complexity of [the] revenue cycle, we know what it takes to improve performance. We’re bringing that expertise together with AI and payer intelligence, and we stand behind the outcomes. This is the level of accountability health systems should expect from their revenue management partners.”.

OpenEvidence unveiled Wednesday the launch of Access Intelligence, a slate of tools built directly into its platform that allows clinicians to access affordability and coverage information.

Access Intelligence is free to all clinicians and can answer questions about availability and eligibility on more than 2,500 patient support programs, like copay savings and patient assistance, the tech giant notes. Other key features include:.

The company says the suite will “continue to evolve to best support clinicians through the complex affordability and coverage landscape.”.

In a recent development, “Programs exist to help patients with treatment access, and prior authorizations can be won, but the process is so fragmented and time-consuming that engaging with it is nearly impossible,” said Ania Bilski, M.D., OpenEvidence clinical AI vice president, in a statement. “Access Intelligence is our commitment to helping physicians and patients close the loop of care, from identifying support programs to completing enrollment to getting a prior authorization approved. Choosing the right treatment should be the hard part. Getting the patient access to it shouldn’t be.”.

The Ohio State University and Microsoft confirmed Tuesday a five-year strategic partnership that aims to accelerate innovation across clinical care settings, education and research.

“Artificial intelligence represents one of the most significant opportunities to transform and improve how hospitals care for patients,” said John Warner, M.D., Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center CEO, in a statement. “Through this collaboration, we have an opportunity to help reimagine the future of healthcare as we bring together Ohio State’s academic medical expertise with Microsoft’s technological capabilities to accelerate the pace of innovation across patient care, research and education.”.

Microsoft and the Ohio State Wexner Medical Center are co-developing a smart hospital model through the partnership, while also modernizing clinical and research applications and workloads through the cloud, unifying data and using AI to support care teams.

The American Medical Association (AMA) adopted a policy on Monday that declares AI can be used to aid physicians and assist with clinical tasks, but cannot be granted licensure, professional titles or certifications to practice medicine.

Moreover, the organization mentioned it will advocate for legislation that establishes a framework for physician oversight of AI clinical-decision making. The organization also is calling for protections for physicians when AI tools cause patient harm.

AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., noted in a statement that "patients deserve to know who is responsible for their care.".

"Physicians also need the authority, oversight and liability protections to make independent decisions when AI is part of the care team," Underwood said.

Identity verification company Clear launched Monday two integrations within the Epic Toolbox, which will allow health systems to verify outside providers and prescribing clinicians.

The company’s CLEAR1 identity platform is now available through Epic Toolbox for EpicCare Link and electronic prescribing of controlled substances. The prescribing integration is available in Epic’s End User Authentication category.

In a recent development, “Doctors and nurses shouldn't spend their shifts proving who they are,” mentioned David Bardan, CLEAR SVP, general manager and head of healthcare, in a statement. “Getting into a patient's chart and prescribing a controlled medication are two more places they no longer have to start from scratch. We're using secure identity to make healthcare safer and easier for care teams, from the first day to the first patient, and every shift after.”.

Ellipsis Health, a voice AI care management company, acquired Kouper Health, a startup that built AI agents deeply embedded in clinical workflows.

Kouper's AI agents work inside health system electronic health record (EHR) systems like Athenahealth and Epic to coordinate care from scheduling through discharge and follow-up.

The deal pairs Ellipsis's "emotionally intelligent" AI voice care manager, Sage, with Kouper's native EHR integrations and longitudinal patient maps to deliver continuous, connected patient care, according to the companies.

It has been revealed that ellipsis Health works with seven of the top 20 health plans in the U.S. and leading academic medical centers and integrated delivery networks.

Industry observers note that founded in 2022, Kouper has raised funding from investors including CVS Health Ventures, General Catalyst and 25madison. Its technology embeds AI agents into health system workflows and builds longitudinal patient maps that bring information from across a patient’s care into a more unified view. Ellipsis' Sage can pick up from there with discharge follow-ups, medication adherence support and clinical check-ins by phone and text. Sage is used by nine of the top 15 U.S. health intends and has delivered up to 7x ROI for customers, the company mentioned.

Sage is powered by a patented "empathy engine" trained on over 3 million labeled clinical conversations. It analyzes vocal cues in real time to assess emotional signals and adapt its interactions. Through phone and text, Sage supports care management tasks including enrollment, clinical assessments, medication adherence and post-discharge follow-up.

Kouper’s team is joining Ellipsis. Both companies will continue serving existing customers under their respective brands while developing a combined product roadmap, with new offerings for health systems expected in the months ahead.

“Healthcare has enormous potential to benefit from AI, but the hard part has been making that technology work for patients and care teams,” mentioned Mainul Mondal, founder and CEO of Ellipsis Health, in a statement. “We have extraordinary clinicians, but we can’t solve access and continuity problems by asking them to do more. Kouper brings critical infrastructure for making that possible inside health systems. By combining their native integrations and longitudinal patient maps with Sage’s emotional intelligence, we can help care teams extend their reach and deliver more continuous, personalized support.”.

Sellers Are Cutting Home Prices the Most in These Markets—Led by One ‘Weirdly Nice’ City

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the market slowed in October due to seasonal trends and elevated mortgage rates, more than 1 in 5 listings throughout the country saw a price reduction, the highest October level since 2022.
  • For a few major metros, the share of price-reduced homes has pulled significantly ahead of the national share of listings with price reductions, which stood at 20.5%.
  • Industry observers note that price reductions were most common in Salt Lake City, where a whopping 31.8% of listings had price cuts as of October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the market slowed in October due to seasonal trends and elevated mortgage rates, more than 1 in 5 listings throughout the country saw a price reduction, the highest October level since 2022.

For a few major metros, the share of price-reduced homes has pulled significantly ahead of the national share of listings with price reductions, which stood at 20.5%.

Industry observers note that price reductions were most common in Salt Lake City, where a whopping 31.8% of listings had price cuts as of October. The median listing price in October was $559,000 in Salt Lake City, a 3.5% decrease from October 2025, according to the Realtor.com economic research team’s monthly housing trends report.

The share of price-reduced homes in Salt Lake City increased 1.6 percentage points over last October.

Salt Lake City is followed closely by Indianapolis, where 31.7% of homes have had a price reduction, and Denver, with 30.9%.

Of the 50 largest metro areas in the U.S., these 10 had the largest share of price reductions in October:.

Of these top 10 cities for price reductions, eight also topped the list in October 2025, confirming these are mostly longstanding softer markets, according to Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel.

Raleigh and front-runner Salt Lake City are the latest to join the top 10 cities where price cuts are most frequent.

For Salt Lake City, Indianapolis, Portland, and Denver, price cuts can be common as the weather grows colder and the market has less movement, indicates Krimmel.

“These markets in particular compared to the rest of the list, which is mostly Sun Belt, can be very unfavorable to sellers when the weather gets cold and buyers stay away until spring,” the economist indicates.

The reason for widespread price decreases in Salt Lake City may go a step further, showcasing a unique aspect of the city’s market: Buyers are “weirdly nice,” according to Joel Carson, who has been a real estate agent in the area for over 30 years.

“Utah is very unique in that people don’t lowball offers. They don’t want to offend the seller, so they’ll wait for that price reduction before they offer,” Carson tells Realtor.com. “Sellers are always asking, ‘Why wouldn’t they just offer me less?’ And the reason is that we have weirdly nice people here, and they don’t want to be offensive.”.

For Carson and fellow agents in the area, the understanding of this politeness helps them properly advise sellers.

Recent findings suggest that when the market is slow, like it has been this fall, he tends to take homes he’s listing off the market for 30 days to let them rest. They can then be relisted with fresh days on the market and a significant price reduction.

Recent findings suggest that when buyers are hesitating, pricing ahead of the market is key to staying competitive. By pricing 5% to 8% under current value, listings attract buyers who may be wary of asking for price concessions, according to Carson.

Uncertainty surrounding the midterm elections, elevated mortgage rates, and concerns about affordability slowed October down, with pending sales down 10.5% and contract signings down 17% year over year.

Still, the right price reduction can result in multiple bites from buyers, Carson says.

In a recent development, “Just this last week, we were at $345,000 on a house and we went to $320,000 and got an offer, so we’re under contract. We actually got two offers,” says Carson. “Once you know what your seller’s bandwidth is, I try to do a large price reduction versus these tiny little ones, and it’s very effective.”.

Of the 50 largest metros, 12 saw price cuts on a quarter or more of listings, and 34 are running above their cut rate last year.

Metros where price cuts were the least common in October were New York City at 12.6%; Buffalo, NY, at 13%; and Hartford, CT, at 14.2%.

Breaking: Router In Arkansas Sparked FAA's Nationwide Ground Stop

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (486 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Commercial airline travel has returned to some form of normalcy after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • It has been revealed that the FAA heaped blame for the air traffic control calamity on L3Harris, the defense contractor that owns and operates the telecommunications network that connects America's air traffic control system.
  • Industry observers note that when the FAA lifted the ground stop four hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took to the podium in the White House Press Briefing Room as if they were taking a victory lap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Commercial airline travel has returned to some form of normalcy after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday. With over 9,000 flights canceled, speculation quickly centered on the agency's newly introduced AI air traffic control tools as the cause of the crisis. While AI could easily be ruled out, the actual reason might be just as idiotic. The FAA traced everything back to a router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. The issue was compounded by a similar upgrade made at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, several weeks earlier. A misconfiguration of the new equipment overwhelmed slower, legacy systems across the country with a torrent of data.

It has been revealed that the FAA heaped blame for the air traffic control calamity on L3Harris, the defense contractor that owns and operates the telecommunications network that connects America's air traffic control system. This network is linked by thousands of aging industrial-grade routers that are being replaced by new routers produced by Cisco and Juniper Systems. According to The New York Times, the new routers in Arkansas and Texas "pinged the communications network hundreds of times per second, overwhelming an antiquated system." Agency officials pinpointed the problem to a broadcasting feature on the router. The data deluge caused communications disruptions at 17 of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, forcing officials to call for a nationwide ground stop.

Industry observers note that when the FAA lifted the ground stop four hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took to the podium in the White House Press Briefing Room as if they were taking a victory lap. The duo addressed reporters as if the nation would be grateful the crisis lasted only a few hours, not furious that it happened at all. Duffy panhandled Congress for $50 billion while insisting that there would be more nationwide ground stops otherwise. Mullin had no real answers other than that he wasn't ruling out a cyberattack as a potential cause. Duffy and Mullin seemed more like Rosencrantz and Guildenstern than Cabinet secretaries.

Duffy has already been granted $12.5 billion to modernize the country's air traffic control system. The soaring price tag seems ridiculous for replacing copper with fiber-optic cable, to borrow his often-mentioned line. The FAA knew how massive this project was before it allocated a single dollar to it. The jump to $50 billion raises questions about how Duffy is spending his budget.

To hedge off any conspiracy theories around cybersecurity, the L3Harris-run telecommunications system isn't connected to the internet. A foreign adversary or any other actor would need a person inside an FAA facility to attack the network. An NJ Transit construction crew showed the network is physically vulnerable earlier this year by severing an FAA backup system's fiber-optic cable alongside the Northeast Corridor, but that still wasn't enough to cause nationwide issues.

Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dyania Health is partnering with Nvidia to run its Synapsis AI clinical reasoning platform inside hospitals’ IT systems, enabling large-scale analysis without patient data leaving their networks.

The startup's Synapsis AI reads a patient's full medical record, including clinical notes, imaging and operative reports, labs and other largely unstructured information, and answers clinical questions while pointing back to supporting evidence in the chart. Dyania Health goes beyond summarizing medical records; it uses AI to convert messy, unstructured clinical records into usable datasets and insights.

Nvidia provides the computing infrastructure needed to perform that analysis across potentially entire patient populations behind the hospital firewall, without transferring patient records outside the health system, according to the organization.

Dyania brings the clinical reasoning technology and implementation expertise, while Nvidia brings the accelerated computing platform and the software that lets it run securely and efficiently on-premises, Eirini Schlosser, founder and CEO of Dyania Health, told Fierce Healthcare.

Through this collaboration with Nvidia, Dyania's Synapsis AI could help health systems turn large volumes of unstructured clinical data into actionable insights at a scale that would be impractical with manual chart review, while keeping patient data inside the hospital’s own infrastructure, Schlosser said.

Industry observers note that health systems have vast amounts of valuable clinical information locked in unstructured medical records, but manually reviewing those records makes it difficult to use that data at scale for research, registries and predictive models. Synapsis AI aims to remove that bottleneck by analyzing patients’ records longitudinally, determining what happened and when, and identifying the clinical evidence supporting those conclusions, according to the organization, which launched out of stealth two years ago.

Frontier models are becoming extraordinarily capable, but the architectures, training data sets, as well as logic are not built to perform clinical reasoning in a real-world healthcare system environment, Schlosser noted.

According to recent reports, dyania's Synapsis AI combines specialized models, a clinician-annotated clinical knowledge base, evidence tracing and hospital-specific implementation. Dyania notes it has invested more than 25,000 physician hours annotating medical cases so that Synapsis AI can perform clinical reasoning. This specialized approach is better suited to complex clinical reasoning than a single general-purpose AI model, Schlosser asserted.

"Every patient's story is spread across years of notes, reports and results, and for the first time we can reason across all of it at once, the way a specialist does, for every patient in a health system rather than one chart at a time,” Schlosser said.

Synapsis AI is built on the Nvidia AI enterprise software stack end to end. Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with the Nvidia NeMo framework for model training and reinforcement learning. Inside the health system, Synapsis AI runs on Nvidia TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM on the hospital's own accelerated computing infrastructure, so inference stays inside the hospital's private network.

"Synapsis AI sits within the health system firewall and is small enough to run inference on local clusters of GPU computing. It does not need to 'speak to the internet' or interact with cloud or frontier models. This provides immense benefits to the healthcare systems for both the comparable cost of tokenomics they would be paying for the frontier models in the cloud as well as for cybersecurity and data privacy of sensitive patient data," Schlosser stated. "Hospitals can apply that capability to their patient histories under their own data governance, without sending those records to an external AI service.".

Hospitals can use their own historical patient data to determine which treatments work for which patients, identify care gaps and ultimately recommend the next appropriate action, according to Schlosser.

It has been revealed that under the collaboration, the companies will work to bring Synapsis AI on Nvidia infrastructure to health systems in the U.S. and internationally, publish joint case studies and integrate Synapsis AI with Nvidia's healthcare software stack. The companies are exploring additional Nvidia technologies to secure AI processing, handle multiple clinical workloads at once and scale computing capacity, with the goal of moving from batch processing toward near-real-time clinical insights at the point of care.

According to recent reports, "Health systems need AI they can trust, integrate into their workflows and operate efficiently. That means connecting information across clinical systems, validating performance for the patients they serve, protecting sensitive data and making results useful within the tools clinicians already use," Chelsea Sumner, Nvidia's U.S. healthcare AI startups ecosystem lead, told Fierce Healthcare.

Recent findings suggest that "Dyania’s approach addresses part of that challenge by running inside the hospital’s own environment and linking findings to evidence in the patient record. Scaling also requires clinicians, technology teams and hospital leaders to work together from the start, with clear responsibility for reviewing results and monitoring performance. Success should be measured by whether AI helps teams find patients who need attention, make better-informed decisions and spend more time delivering care," Sumner stated.

Cleveland Clinic used Dyania Health’s Synapsis AI, running on Nvidia infrastructure, to analyze up to 16 years of records from 7,812 aortic valve replacement patients. The study addressed a central concern for patients: How long will the replacement valve last, and will another procedure be needed?

Researchers reviewed nearly 8,000 patient records between 2005 and 2021, mostly narrative notes and echocardiogram reports that registries can struggle to capture.

Industry observers note that "Understanding how a replacement heart valve performs means following a patient across years of care, connecting the original operative report with subsequent progress notes, hospitalizations, echocardiograms, other medical conditions and later interventions. Much of that information is buried in narrative records that researchers would otherwise need to review manually," Schlosser noted.

Industry observers note that the AI extracted information from narrative clinical records and answered 88 questions per patient about their valves, health conditions and subsequent care. Each answer linked to supporting evidence in the chart, he noted.

Researchers used that dataset to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and the risk of another intervention. The model estimates valve deterioration and repeat-procedure risk at three, five and 10 years post-procedure, with estimates that update as upcoming medical information about the patient becomes available.

"Historically, this would have required human manual abstraction, and for 7,812 patients, it would be humanly impossible to read and abstract features on an ongoing basis at the rate at which medical records are changing. Additionally, humans reading a medical record can often miss information if they skim through it," Schlosser mentioned.

The tool is used to help inform care but requires external validation from clinicians.

It has been revealed that "Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients," stated Lars G. Svensson, M.D., Ph.D., chief of the Heart, Vascular and Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic, in a statement.

The health system began working with Dyania Health a year ago to use its AI platform for clinical trial recruitment.

Synapsis AI made it possible for the first time to comprehensively analyze nearly two decades of patient data, Schlosser asserted. "What was even more groundbreaking was the ability to go from raw data in unstructured form to predictive risk models in one fell swoop. This enables precision care at scale and empowers physicians with stronger sets of information backing their clinical decisions about any given patient, including questions like 'when should the patient have their next echo?' or 'when will the patient likely need a reintervention?'" Schlosser noted.

The Cleveland Clinic and Dyania Health collaboration reflects Nvidia's broader focus to provide healthcare and life sciences innovators with the computing platform and AI tools to advance research and help care teams better understand patients’ needs, Sumner mentioned.

The heart valve study shows how Synapsis AI could help health systems use their own patient data to determine which treatments work best for which patients and improve predictive models over time, ultimately supporting more personalized care recommendations, according to Dyania Health.

Industry observers note that "Nvidia's infrastructure enables us to handle more work concurrently and use resources more efficiently. That could allow hospitals to examine larger populations, ask more detailed questions and revisit analyses more frequently. The longer-term opportunity is to move from periodic batches of records toward insights available closer to the moment a clinician needs them," Schlosser said.

"We can do that within the health system’s own environment, keeping patient records behind its firewall. We are also evaluating capabilities for distributed inference, workload isolation and protection of data during computation. Computing power alone does not make a clinical conclusion correct; it allows a carefully developed clinical system to work at greater scale and speed," he remarked.

Sumner asserts that healthcare organizations are just scratching the surface on the potential for AI to uncover clinically useful information buried in longitudinal patient records.

Sources indicate that "Connecting a physician’s notes with earlier test results and treatment history could help identify patients who need follow-up, match people with clinical trials and give researchers a clearer understanding of how treatments perform over time," she said. "The Cleveland Clinic heart valve study is a concrete example. AI helped researchers assemble a detailed view of patients’ care to study how replacement valves deteriorate. The opportunity is to turn that knowledge into more personalized monitoring and better-informed care decisions. Clinicians need to be able to review the supporting evidence, validate the findings and decide what they mean for each patient.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that generally, I don't recommend stealing from your employer, and if you're going to do it, try to be discreet at the very least. Unfortunately, one Ford employee didn't heed that advice, and now he and three other folks are in a heap of trouble. For six weeks in the spring of 2025, Stratec Auto in Detroit received deliveries of brand fresh parts straight from Ford's Rouge Complex every Saturday night... until Ford security caught on.

It has been revealed that now, the four men are charged with stealing well over $80,000 in parts from the Dearborn, Michigan, factory, Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy told Automotive News. 35-year-old Wissam Faraj reportedly took parts from the Rogue factory where he worked, to give them to 63-year-old Badr Kahil and his sons, 25-year-old Aiman and 36-year-old Firas. The men allegedly sold the stolen parts through the repair shop and on eBay.

Industry observers note that one of the Kahils would simply place an order for parts with Faraj for him to steal from Ford. From there, he'd simply take them and deliver the parts to the shop. Worthy described the scheme as "lucrative, shameless and absolutely illegal.".

According to recent reports, ford began its investigation after other employees at the plant noticed parts were going missing, which isn't something that typically happens. From there, The Blue Oval notified Dearborn police, who arranged a sort of sting operation. Officers set up a controlled purchase for more parts to catch the men in the act. They also looked at thousands of texts, emails, photos, videos, and various online accounts, according to FOX 2 Detroit.

It's actually possible that the value of the stolen parts could end up being significantly greater than what was listed in the charges, because it's so hard to track everything down. Worthy pointed to a text message from Faraj that referenced one order for 128 sets of headlights that totaled $22,400 on its own. It's very possible that the number could reach into the "millions," FOX 2 reports. Worthy described it as "a very large amount of money.".

Here's what Ford said about the matter in a statement to FOX 2 Detroit:.

"Ford's Global Security team launched a thorough investigation after notification of suspected theft and unauthorized sale of tech giant parts at two manufacturing facilities. While we do not comment on individual personnel matters, the team conducted a comprehensive review of the incident and implemented corrective actions to strengthen security measures at our sites. The company will continue to work with local authorities throughout the investigation.".

Faraj, unsurprisingly, was fired in 2025.
