📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that zion* was little more than a stranger when he lifted me up onto his lap in one swift movement. His hands were sure, yet soft, as he held my face, kissing me deeply. After a few moments, I pulled back, then looked down, unsure of how to respond to what I could feel was his obvious desire for sex.

I wanted him. But I was afraid I didn’t know how to do this.

Zion was the second man I’d been with since my divorce, but he was the first one I actually liked—and that I wanted to like me back.

Recent findings suggest that sensing my insecurity, Zion tipped my chin to his mouth and kissed me softer. With my legs wrapped around his waist, he picked me up and carried me to his bedroom. I threw my head back, curls wild, and giggled in a way I hadn’t in over a decade of being married.

As our bodies tangled together, our breathing synced, he looked me directly in the eyes and asked, “Are you ok? How does this feel?” I had never had a man check in with me like that.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel so safe with you,” I whispered into Zion’s ear. It surprised me to know how true that was since we’d only met a few hours ago. I’d been sitting alone at a bar, as had he, and we’d struck up a casual conversation that promptly turned intimate.

Industry observers note that I hadn’t felt safe in a long time. Not since sex with my ex-husband had become less like something I looked forward to each week and more like a duty I dreaded.

Recent findings suggest that throughout our 13-year marriage, I felt like I had expectations placed on me and my body as a wife—my husband’s “needs” often seemed to supersede my own. Consent felt implied. I didn’t think I could say “no” because that might be met with anger or coercive tactics, like begging me over and over until I relented. Each time, my sense of safety and trust eroded.

Eventually, I started recoiling from my husband’s touch because it felt like every hug or little neck rub would turn into him wanting sex.

Sources indicate that naturally, my libido took a nosedive. I thought the problem was me, so I went to sex therapy. But as I started to explore myself in those sessions, I realized I was still sexual. In fact, I was highly sexual. I just didn’t want to have sex with him because I always felt hypervigilant for my emotional and physical safety.

Sources indicate that after two months of sex therapy, I asked my ex to sleep in a separate bedroom. Then, I asked for the separation that led to our divorce.

In the early stages of my separation, I was tempted to swear off sex—and men—entirely. This is not uncommon, claims Laura Sgro, LCSW, an anxiety and trauma therapist in Los Angeles. “Many women are like ‘screw men,’ because it’s a fear-based response,” she explains. “They’ve learned over time, especially in long-term marriages, to associate sex and intimacy with something that’s not going to be pleasurable for them, with something that’s not really their choice.”.

Additionally, love and relationship coaches on social media often suggest celibacy as a way to heal after divorce and sexual trauma. But what if casual sex is the antidote many women need instead?

Once the stress of the divorce dissipated and I settled into my new life as a single mother, I just wanted to have some fun. So, I started leaving my house more often, instead of being wrapped up in “mom duties” all of the time. I went to cute cafes to work, had lunch or drinks at a bar, smiled at men who looked at me, and started conversations with people around me. That’s how I met Zion, and, well, one thing led to another….

According to recent reports, although I liked him—immediately—I wasn’t looking for commitment. Being someone’s partner or girlfriend didn’t sound appealing to me because I’d just escaped all the oppressive gendered expectations that had come with those labels. I just wanted to feel desired and have sex again—uninhibited, no strings attached, exploratory, and pleasurable. I wanted to be free.

In a recent development, casual sex can be a way for women to take their agency back, says Alica Livingston, a licensed marriage and family therapist based in Texas. “When sex becomes their choice—who they have sex with, when they have sex, what that sex looks like—it can be an incredibly healing and powerful experience.”.

It can also be an informative one. Many women don’t know what they like in the bedroom because so much of their sexual experience has been framed around their partner’s pleasure, says Sgro. Embracing casual sex after a breakup or divorce can help women center their own pleasure and regain their confidence.

Industry observers note that but if you want to get to know your body better before jumping into bed with someone new, try some solo exploration. “Experimenting with self-touch, even non-sexually, can help women identify what they actually like and dislike,” indicates Sgro. She suggests touching yourself in ways you haven't tried before—light, firm, slow, still—and rate sensations as pleasant, neutral, or not for you. (For example, you might enjoy gently trailing your finger along the inside of your forearm, but want a firmer touch around your erogenous zones.) Over time, this self-exploration can expand into more sensual territory, like trying toys that offer different sensations or inviting a partner to explore further.

Sgro also recommends women find a hobby or activity that helps them connect with their bodies. “Many women feel disconnected from their bodies post-divorce, and it's so crucial to rebuild that connection with yourself on your terms,” she indicates. It can be yoga, weight lifting, dance classes—anything that helps you feel stronger, more empowered, and able to express yourself through movement.

For me, it was twerk classes. The rap music reminded me of the ’90s video vixens and my first “hoe phase” in high school. As a young woman, I had a lot of unsatisfying, performative sex out of pressure to be cool and feel chosen.

Recent findings suggest that this, of course, is the argument against casual sex, and why embracing it often goes against the popular #BoySober and “decentering men” movements. These trends are not only a direct response to the violence women risk by romantically interacting with men; they are also evidence of the humiliating and lackluster dating dynamics we face now—breadcrumbing, micro-cheating, future faking, monkey branching (the Gen Z-informed list goes on).

Recent findings suggest that it’s also true that more women than men experience postcoital dysphoria and regret after one-night stands, booty calls, and casual sexual encounters. But this isn’t just another case of the classic gender gap—it’s due to a variety of factors, not least of which is sexual satisfaction.

But casual sex that is intentional, focused on self-exploration, and re-centers your pleasure can take off the pressure to perform or please your partner, notes Sgro.

Now that I was in my late 30s, I was determined that my second “hoe phase” would be all about me and what I wanted. For starters, I wrote down my “Hell Yes” and “Hell No” lists. It was an easy and straightforward way for me to figure out what I liked in bed, what I wanted to try, and what I wasn’t open to. I also used sexting to get more comfortable sharing my desires and boundaries with newly introduced partners, which was great practice for having those conversations in person.

Sources indicate that for me, having a post-divorce “hoe phase” was exactly what I needed. I started having the best sex of my life, including with Zion. He was the first man I saw myself with post-divorce, but neither of us were ready for a commitment at the time, so our connection only lasted a few weeks. For the next three years, I entertained many casual romantic and sexual connections. Eventually, I realized that while having no-strings-attached sex was great, I love monogamy and would like to get married again. So, earlier this year, I started seriously dating someone else.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, it didn’t work out, and I recently became single again. Part of me wonders if I should have another “hoe phase”? Or, should I stay away from random men until I find my husband?

Recent findings suggest that sgro indicates any woman going through a divorce or a breakup should ask herself these kinds of questions—and be honest in her answers. “If you want casual sex, give yourself that permission to explore it in a way that feels good for you,” she says. “And if you’re not ready for that, that’s OK too. No one makes the rules except you.”.

Sources indicate that so, I don’t know if I’ll continue to embrace casual sex, take some time to explore celibacy, or perhaps return to a past romance. What I do know is that my “hoe phase” opened possibilities—for more autonomy and more pleasure. And maybe even love.

Sources indicate that tech giant Apple rolled out the Apple Health AI Usage Study today with prepares to recruit 200,000 participants in the U.S. to gain a better understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools.

In a recent development, the study is open to individuals 21 or older who live in the U.S., and participants must have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later. Apple will run the virtual research study on a dedicated Apple Health AI Study App, separate from the Apple Health and Research apps. Participants may remain in the study for up to 12 months, Apple remarked.

Industry observers note that by examining what drives user trust, the quality of responses, comprehension and everyday health actions, the study aims to inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for Apple and the industry, the manufacturer said. There are also privacy implications that need to be explored, Apple representatives said. Researchers also want to evaluate how AI chatbots complement the traditional healthcare system and the handoff to physicians.

The tech organization is collaborating with OpenEvidence on the research initiative, as the startup provides the underlying clinical AI technology for Apple’s Health AI Usage Study. OpenEvidence is a widely used AI-powered clinical decision support tool and medical search engine for clinicians. The company's platform pulls directly from licensed, peer-reviewed literature and clinical guidelines through formal partnerships with The Upcoming England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), JAMA, Nature, Cochrane, and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN).

Apple said it selected OpenEvidence as a partner for its high-quality medical sources, robust privacy controls, and advanced search models.

According to recent reports, through Apple’s study app, participants can ask everyday health questions and receive answers in approachable language, with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources, Apple said. Users can ask about symptoms, general health questions, recovery from procedures, fitness and other health concerns. They can rate the AI's answers and indicate what was useful or lacking, Apple said.

Industry observers note that study participants can also choose to share HealthKit data types—such as resting heart rate, activity and sleep—to get more personalized responses to health questions. If study participants have imported clinical records into the Health app and separately agree to share them with the Health AI Usage study, the app can incorporate that information, primarily lab results, Apple representatives mentioned.

Industry observers note that "At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey," Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement.

Apple described the research initiative as a formal study overseen by an independent review board.

Participants will complete a mandatory onboarding process that includes informed consent, and they'll be asked to share demographic information such as age, race and education so researchers can examine how these variables affect participant preferences and communication needs, Apple mentioned.

The company mentioned study participants will receive baseline and monthly surveys, allowing researchers to examine how people use the information they receive and what happens afterward.

The Health AI Usage study app also includes tools to help people prepare for healthcare appointments, along with surveys after visits to gauge whether the use of health AI chatbots makes patients feel better prepared or empowered and improves their interactions with providers, Apple stated.

The study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency and clinical guardrails, the manufacturer noted. Study data will not be used to train AI models, Apple confirmed.

Industry observers note that apple said it has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information. User queries on the Health AI Usage Study app are first processed on the iPhone to remove identifying information. The queries then flow to a secure study environment managed by a third-party study support contractor where they are de-linked from individual participant IDs and screened again before being sent to OpenEvidence where answers are generated using supporting reference materials, Apple said.

The study app also features safety guardrails that are intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed.

Industry observers note that consumers are increasingly using general AI chatbots powered by LLMs to get answers to health questions. But research indicates a wide gap exists between an AI's technical accuracy and a patient's ability to safely use that information.

"Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds. When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Connecting these tools, and rigorously studying what works, is how we’ll get there," Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, noted in a statement.

According to recent reports, the Health AI Usage study builds on Apple's growing research initiatives. In 2019, the company released its Research app and three medical studies to test how well its Apple Watch can track a person's mobility and cardiovascular health, changes in hearing and women's health and fertility. Last year, it began the Apple Health Study to use its devices, including iPhones, Apple Watch and AirPods along with third-party devices, for a longitudinal, virtual study to monitor changes in participants’ health, spanning a wide range of health and disease areas.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Las Vegas drowns in unsold homes and priced-out buyers sit on the sidelines waiting for lower mortgage rates, the luxury rental sector is booming, fueled by visiting celebrities, professional athletes, and out-of-town millionaires eyeing a permanent move.

In October, Las Vegas’ overall housing inventory reached an all-time high of nearly 11,450 units, up roughly 10% compared to a year ago, as mortgage rates topping 7% left many buyers priced out.

Yet at the very top of the local rental market, the exact opposite is happening.

Local brokers say that demand for rental mansions in Las Vegas and neighboring Henderson, NV, priced between $50,000 to $100,000 per month is severely outstripping supply.

"In the ultraluxury rental space, there's a huge shortage," Natalia Harris, global real estate adviser with Las Vegas Sotheby's International Realty, tells Realtor.com®. There are currently fewer than 10 super-luxury rentals on the market.

"We personally, day to day, feel the frustrations of the shortage of the inventory of these rentals, because we get requests and we can't even keep up with them.".

Harris and her husband, fellow Sotheby's adviser Ben Harris, have been actively encouraging developers and investors to create more extravagant rental inventory to keep up with demand.

In a recent development, well-heeled medium-term renters, including NFL stars and elite entertainers with $1 million-per-show residencies on the iconic Vegas Strip, are not just looking for a place to sleep. They crave complete privacy, top-of-the-line accommodations, and customized features ranging from branded basketball courts to on-site tour bus hookups.

Alongside celebrity renters, the Harrises often work with out-of-town executives and entrepreneurs who are considering a relocation to Las Vegas but are not sure where exactly to put down roots.

"They're renting for a year maybe, or six months, while they're browsing and shopping for a home and figuring out where they want to be," says Natalia. This class of clients gravitates toward rentals in the $50,000- to $60,000-per-month bracket.

While in the past the biggest feeder market for high-end rentals in Vegas was California, Natalia claims over the past year, momentum has shifted to Seattle. Wealthy Washington residents are increasingly eyeing tax-friendly Nevada following the recent passage of the "millionaires tax"—a 9.9% state income tax on earnings exceeding $1 million a year.

Behind this premium rental surge is the valley's rapidly rising cultural cachet.

"Vegas used to be a place where you get a cheap dinner and you gamble, maybe catch a show. But now, Vegas has become the sports and entertainment capital," indicates Natalia.

In recent years, Las Vegas has cemented its reputation as a top destination for world-class sports, culminating with hosting Super Bowl LVIII in 2024.

In a recent development, the city's jam-packed calendar includes the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, the NASCAR Cup Series, college football and basketball tournaments, and high-stakes championship boxing. In 2028, Vegas will host the NCAA Men’s Final Four, followed the next year by Super Bowl LXIII.

Beyond headline-making marquee spectacles, Las Vegas has built a thriving local sports scene anchored by championship franchises like the Stanley Cup-winning Vegas Golden Knights and the WNBA champion Las Vegas Aces.

It has been revealed that "Vegas has completely evolved, and the attention that we're getting from high net worth individuals ... or celebrities and athletes that are coming here for some of those events, it's just created a whole new dynamic," states Natalia.

Sports is not the city's only draw. As part of the valley's cultural evolution, the Strip has been increasingly attracting A-list entertainers at the peak of their careers, marking a major shift from decades past.

"Vegas used to be a place where artists came when they were toward the end of their career," claims Natalia. "Elvis, Frank Sinatra—they would come here as they're winding down for their residencies. Now, that's not the case at all.".

The city's most prestigious fresh venue, the Sphere, has recently featured Backstreet Boys, Metallica, and U2. Pink and John Mayer are slated for upcoming residencies.

It has been revealed that "For us in the rental space, that's really where we're seeing our demand, because these artists aren't people that can just walk through the hotel and grab some dinner and be unnoticed and left alone," notes Natalia. "They're going to be swarmed by fans wanting photos, and they need somewhere where they can escape while they're in Vegas.".

Affluent clients working with Natalia and her husband often travel with family and aides, and they seek a refuge from the frenzy of the Strip, which they can find in guard-gated golf course communities nestled in the mountains just 15 minutes outside city center.

"A lot of them don't realize there's life off the Strip," states Ben. "Once they find out about that and they stay once, they want to keep coming back.".

It has been revealed that demand for luxury rentals in the valley predictably spikes around major events. During the Super Bowl, the Harrises secured accommodations for the families of five top starters from both the San Francisco 49ers and the Kansas City Chiefs.

Summer is a particularly busy season, drawing NBA players to town for the Summer League or off-season workouts at the elite IMPACT Basketball training facility.

These high-profile clients typically rent mansions for one to three months in ultraexclusive enclaves like MacDonald Highlands—a 1,320-acre master-planned golf community nestled in the foothills of the Black and McCullough mountains in Henderson.

The undisputed poster child for this sector of the market is 750 Dragon Ridge Drive in Henderson, which the Harrises rented out for a record-setting $100,000 per month.

"That one is the star of the show. Everybody's first choice would be that one," Natalia says of the compound-style, 13,000-square-foot property shielded by three separate security gates to guarantee complete privacy.

In a recent development, the 2.2-acre property features indoor and outdoor basketball courts, a gym, a tennis court, a bowling alley, a spa, and a tour bus hookup that Ben and Natalia had installed at the request of visiting performers. It also includes a separate structure with additional bedrooms and en suite bathrooms to house a celebrity's entourage.

"It's not just one person coming on their own," indicates Natalia. "They have chefs, they have trainers, they have security. So having a high bedroom count and a floor proposal that can accommodate their teams while still providing privacy for each other is something that's really huge.".

Beyond the square footage and high-end finishes, the most coveted amenity among most major-name Vegas renters is a panoramic view of the glittering Strip.

"Just like if you're going on a beach vacation, you want to make sure your hotel has the oceanfront views, they want to make sure they have that unobstructed Strip view so they can pull out their phone and FaceTime somebody like, 'I told you I'm doing it major in Las Vegas, look at this view of the Strip at night shining.'".

For the Harrises, witnessing their A-list clients take in that view for the first time never gets old.

In a recent development, "It doesn't matter how massive the celebrity is, they still get so excited," says Natalia. "And it's so fun to watch that 'awe' moment when they walk into the home and just have the panoramic view of the Las Vegas Strip in front of them. That's our favorite moment.".

It has been revealed that there are some exceptions, though. Ben shared an anecdote about how, on one occasion, the aides of an unnamed Grammy winner who was staying in town insisted that all the windows be completely blacked out so he could get a good night's rest before his show the following day.

"I'm in there trying to show them the amazing views, and they're like, 'No, we can't see anything but black.' I'm like, 'Oh, just peek out for a second, please!'" he recalls with a laugh.

Once the rental agreement is signed, keeping the world-famous renters happy is the main objective.

"One of the reasons people like to rent through us is because we don't really say no," indicates Natalia. "If they want something, we make it work. All these homes are definitely dialed in and ready to go, but sometimes people have things that are really special to them.".

Typical requests include providing a specific brand of mattress or bed, installing a cold plunge, or reconfiguring the space to create more bedrooms for staff.

Other times, the customization requests are purely for fun, such as painting an NBA team's logo on the basketball court at 750 Dragon Ridge Drive.

In a recent development, "You've got to make it happen at these price points," claims Ben. "'No' is not an acceptable answer.".

Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

According to recent reports, if you live by the "ball is life" moniker and you need to be able to play at home, a portable basketball hoop is a must. Portable basketball hoops don't require you to perform manual labor like digging a huge hole in the ground and pouring concrete, nor do they cost over a thousand bucks. Another plus to going portable? You can store your hoop come winter, thus lengthening its lifespan. It’s also a solid option for those who don't have the time, money, or space to install an in-ground option but still wanna toss their basketball shoes on and shoot around a bit quickly.

"I feel like the portable hoop is what transformed me into who I am," NBA shooting coach Chris Matthews (a.k.a. Lethal Shooter) claims. You can make memories like that in whatever space you have for the court. But don't get caught buying a hoop that’s a waste of money. Not all hoops are the same, so we’re here to cut through the noise. Here are some of the best options we came up with.

Industry observers note that spalding makes a handful of portable goals, but the Momentous EZ is our favorite due to its value-driven price and ease of assembly. Recent findings suggest that as Matthews notes, "The more portable a basketball hoop is, the better, so that everyone can move it. That's one reason I like the models from Spalding.".

According to recent reports, as for the materials in the hoop, the Momentous EZ comes with an acrylic backboard in either 50- or 54-inch sizing. You can also choose between a clear view back, an H-frame, or a steel H-frame (for added support and durability). We chose the steel H-frame to help prevent backboard damage. The theory behind the H-frame is that it should help absorb stress when someone dunks or hangs on the rim.

In a recent development, there's a hand crank for adjusting the height of the goal (simple to use if you have kids or if you want to do a driveway dunk contest). The base is wide and supportive and will hold up to 26 gallons of water or sand. If you're looking for a premium goal that won't set you back a thousand dollars, there's nothing better than this pick. Start here in your search. You won't regret it.

More: The 6 Best Basketballs for Indoor Games and Street Hoops.

This means it appeals to everyone from small kids to adults. One cool idea you can do with this goal is you can lower it to its 4-foot setting and position it up against an in-ground pool—something other goals in this guide don't have a low enough range to make it suitable for pool hoops.

One way to help preserve this goal, though, is to store it inside whenever possible to avoid weathering.

The hand crank makes adjusting the goal from 7.5 feet to 10 feet smoother and easier than the turning hand crank on the Spalding EZ goal.

In a recent development, the FORZA Adjustable Basketball Hoop and Post System earns its place as a “Best Adjustable Hoop for Growing Players” thanks to its flexible height settings and portable design. Built for both kids learning their first shots and adults looking for competitive backyard games, the hoop adjusts from youth-friendly heights to regulation size, making it a long-term investment rather than something your kids quickly outgrow. Its wheeled base also makes it easy to move across driveways or patios, adding convenience for families who want flexibility.

Designed for indoor or outdoor use, the hoop features a sturdy base and adjustable frame that can accommodate players of different ages and skill levels. This versatile hoop can come out when you're hosting weekend family games or serious practice sessions, but be stored when not in use. There are also optional upgrades available.

According to recent reports, this model from IE Sports will help save you some cash while still providing decent play. We think it's an awesome feature, as it maximizes solo practice by allowing you to work on passing and catch-and-shoot drills. Overall, this goal is reliable, well-priced, and comes with a fun feature.

It has been revealed that remember how fun mini hoops are? This goal takes mini hoops to a whole other level with an adjustable height pole (up to 7 feet) and a sturdy base. Sure you could buy a cheap sub-$100 full size goal for your kids to play with, but for a similar price you get a much better build and a whole lot of fun.

Position it up to your pool for water mini hoops. Bring it down to your basement or put it in the garage for winter mini hoops. You get the point.

The Huupe Mini Hoop is the perfect nostalgia pick for any guy, regardless of age. It is quite literally the most portable hoop on our list, with the ability to be tossed on any door. This smart hoop has a wide variety of virtual games you can enjoy. The hoop comes with some heft, namely from the technology, which allows you to test your shot against others online, or even watch your favorite streaming apps.

Recent findings suggest that "I think that mini hoops like the Huupe are another great option for families that don't have room in their garage or a driveway," Matthews says. "It's a great way to have kids to get energy out during the day, even when the weather is not ideal. They are easy to install, too.".

In any case, it's easily installed using the classic over-the-door mount. You can also wall mount, but you need to buy those parts separately. There are special sensors throughout the device, which follow your shot as well as your distance from the hoop. This means it can reliably track your shot so you can get better after every game. One of our testers even mentioned, "I enjoyed using this hoop to shoot around with my toddler daughter, and when I just wanted to play around a little bit by myself, it was awesome to get to watch the NBA playoffs on the screen as I shot.".

Chris Matthews (aka Lethal Shooter) is a world-renowned shooting coach to NBA stars like Jaylen Brown, Dwight Howard, and Anthony Davis, and WNBA star Candice Parker.

Having spent countless hours as kids growing up playing pickup games in driveways, we know a thing or two about a solid portable basketball hoop. Men's Health Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, has played lots of basketball and helped us dial in on the proper picks for this guide. Considering all those firsthand experiences led us to find the best of the best. Factors like backboard material, adjustability, and special design notes were considered in our selection process. We also took into account price, as some basketball goals provide a better overall value than others.

According to recent reports, in addition, we also consulted world-renowned basketball shooting coach Chris Matthews (a.k.a. Lethal Shooter) on what makes for a good portable hoop. Our guide below represents our top picks, all approved by Matthews, of portable basketball hoops that will actually last for years to come. Keep scrolling to learn more.

Not every hoop is going to have the same adjustability in terms of how low or high you can raise it. This is crucial if you have little ones and want the whole family to partake in the fun. It’s also a great way to put on a dunk contest if you still have the bunnies, too. There are also different mechanisms built for adjusting, such as a hand crank, a telescoping pole, pneumatic assist, or a gas spring.

The types of materials used directly impact the long-term durability of your hoop. The two types of backboard materials to know about for portable basketball goals are acrylic and polycarbonate (there's also glass, but glass is used for professional backboards and is extremely rare on portable ones). Polycarbonate is going to be cheaper, but the tradeoff is that exposure to weather and UV light will make the backboard brittle and rigid over time. Acrylic is typically more expensive, but the benefit is that it's better suited for exposure to weather and UV light (acrylic is not affected by UV light like polycarbonate), plus you get a more responsive bounce.

Basketball rims are not all created equal. If you’ve ever been to a park court, you know what we mean—one slightly off shot and your ball rockets across the street. There are a few common materials you’ll see: steel and double-rimmed steel, powder-coated rims, and occasionally composite or plastic. You’ll also see that there are breakaway rims, standard, and flex.

To keep a portable basketball hoop in place, you'll need to fill its base with something. Most portable goals hold about 35 gallons, and you can either go with water or sand. We prefer sand because it dissipates well. Sand is also denser than water, so filling the base with sand is wiser for a more secure hold. However, choosing water makes it easier to empty the base and refill, making it easier to maneuver, especially if you need to move elsewhere in your driveway (or take it to your neighbor's for a friendly pickup game).

Recent findings suggest that if you're curious about how much weight you need to keep your goal in place, a safe number is around 300 to 450 pounds. It sounds like a lot, but if you want to be safe and protect your goal, then more weight is always worth adding. And keep in mind that they all include wheels attached to the base to move them more easily. If you want to eliminate the labor of filling the base full, you can fill it to a point and then stack sandbags on top of the back of the goal to keep it in place. It won't be the most pleasing to look at, but it will allow you to move the goal around more easily.

Paying more gets you a better playing experience, especially when it comes to a wide acrylic backboard. A wider backboard makes it easier to shoot bank shots and perform layups, and the acrylic material will be much more responsive and last longer. A more expensive goal might also come with better wheels for moving the goal. Keep in mind a portable basketball hoop won't be as deluxe as an in-ground one, but you can get pretty dang close.

Recent findings suggest that A regulation backboard is typically 48 inches tall by 72 inches wide. Most portable hoops have a 48-inch height, but there's a variance on width. While 72 inches is fun to play on due to the full ability to shoot bank shots and layups, a driveway goal doesn't need to be that wide.

Look to a 50-inch or 54-inch width. Anything under 50 is fine; however, you will lose space to shoot bank shots and layups. The benefit to buying a goal with a smaller backboard, though, is that you save money (they're almost always cheaper).

The easiest way to store a portable basketball goal is to lower the rim to its lowest setting, tarp it, then roll it into a garage or shed. Some basketball hoops can be disassembled (or at least partially disassembled), but that process can be pretty annoying. Make sure to drain any water from the base to avoid it freezing and expanding the plastic of the base.

Some of the high-end Spalding portable goals can partially disassemble for storage (not the Spalding EZ we recommend, though). You can take out bolts at the middle of the goal, and the backboard will fold down, thus helping store it in a garage or shed with a low ceiling.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected fresh approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease.
  • The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear.
  • Industry observers note that the study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected fresh approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

Industry observers note that the study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk.

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

In a recent development, people who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an vital warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin remarked. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease.".

An Anti-Aging Drug Reveals Promise.

Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research revealed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Sources indicate that brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits.

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

It has been revealed that women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

Industry observers note that "We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she mentioned. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most.".

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments.

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

In a recent development, at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more promptly.

Industry observers note that the latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.

Industry observers note that before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was released in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

Industry observers note that to break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it notes. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

Industry observers note that schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Sources indicate that furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Noom pushes deeper into connected health with new wearable, Noom Band" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Noom released its own wearable to enhance its metabolic health platform with activity, sleep and cardiovascular data insights.

In a recent development, the device, called Noom Band, will be bundled into Noom’s existing enterprise partnerships at no additional upfront cost starting in early 2027. The wearable is also free for Noom Health employer and health initiative customers.

The introduction of a wearable is part of Noom’s broader push to build an integrated metabolic health platform combining behavior change, virtual care, diagnostics, medications and continuous health data.

According to recent reports, noom Band is a faceless wrist-worn wearable powered by Sensor Bio, and it will be fully integrated into the Noom app. The device will track heart rate, heart rate variability, SpO2, sleep and activity, with the data feeding directly into Noom’s behavior change platform, executives stated.

Noom is providing the wearable to enterprise clients at no additional upfront cost as it sees opportunities to use continuous data on sleep, activity and other physiological signals to keep members engaged and drive better outcomes in the organization's weight management and metabolic health programs, Noom CEO Geoff Cook told Fierce Healthcare.

"We are getting outcomes-based payments, so we believe we will have more people hitting their 5% weight loss goals or 10% weight loss goals, if they have the wearable, than if they don't," Cook said in an exclusive interview about the launch of Noom Band.

Integrating a wearable device into Noom’s metabolic health program fills a major data gap, Cook mentioned.

Noom has evolved from a weight loss app into a broader preventive care and clinical health platform. The company's behavior change platform uses psychology, clinical support and structured habit design to help customers build long-term lifestyle shifts. The company also offers integrated telehealth services through its Noom Med platform, combining remote clinical care and prescription weight loss medications with its core behavior change app. And the company has expanded into at-home diagnostics with its Biomarkers Test Kit.

Sources indicate that but Noom lacked continuous physiological information, particularly around sleep and activity, Cook said. Less than 10% of members have devices such as the Oura Ring, Whoop, or newer Fitbits, he noted. Continuous physiological data enables Noom to be a more comprehensive healthcare platform.

"This is all about just boosting signal so that we can deliver the right insights, and to do that, we felt we needed to bring a wearable deeper into our program," he said.

Noom is starting with the Noom Band as a wrist-based wearable, and the firm is at an “earlier stage exploring ring-based options,” Cook remarked. "We believe ultimately it’s key to meet people where they are, and both the wrist and the ring form factors have a role to play in generating signal to drive health outcomes, as people have different preferences," he added.

Cook sees chronic care, telehealth, diagnostics and wearable companies increasingly converging as they broaden their capabilities and move into adjacent areas of healthcare.

"Every player in preventive health, which is looking more and more like healthcare generally, is chasing this same holy grail of determining what is going on in a patient or member’s body, and then suggesting a behavioral insight or a pharmaceutical intervention, or ordering a diagnostic test based on that signal," he remarked.

Noom is making strategic moves to cover all of those capabilities itself.

It has been revealed that the company focuses on whole person health that goes beyond nutrition, Cook said, with extensive data and interventions around food and activity but comparatively little insight into sleep. Sleep is an vital factor for metabolic health, and the Noom Band gives the company a way to incorporate sleep alongside nutrition, activity and mindset, executives said.

Noom is betting that wearables can improve outcomes for members in its weight loss programs. An analysis of 144,000 Noom Med members taking a GLP-1 medication found that those who used a connected wearable were 34% more likely to lose 20 pounds by the fourth month in the program, according to the firm. A separate sleep analysis found that, on average, members on a GLP-1 weight loss drug who used Noom Band slept 90 minutes more per week after only two months, and members who started with a sleep deficit added 150 minutes of sleep per week, the company's data shows.

Studies have shown that chronic sleep restriction or poor quality sleep significantly increases the risk of insulin resistance, obesity and type 2 diabetes.

"Bringing that dimension of health into the program, we felt, was just critically crucial," Cook said.

It has been revealed that the company built a device from the ground up rather than partner with an existing wearable player, so it could own the user experience. "We didn't want to pick a partner where essentially that partner’s app would be competing essentially with the Noom application for this signal interpretation," Cook noted.

Many existing wearables focus on optimizing health and athletic performance, Cody Fair, Noom Health’s chief commercial officer, told Fierce Healthcare. Noom developed Noom Band to capture measurements related to weight management and metabolic health, he noted.

In a recent development, through the partnership with Sensor Bio, the wearable platform provides the validated sensors and underlying physiological data, while Noom controls how those signals are interpreted and incorporated into the interventions. Cook cited Sensor Bio's research, validation work and focus on device accuracy as key reasons Noom selected Sensor Bio as its partner to develop Noom Band.

By investing in a wearable, Noom also aims to improve member engagement to ultimately drive better outcomes for the members as well as payers and employers, Fair noted.

It has been revealed that members can lose motivation when the number on the scale stops moving. Giving them other measures of progress, including sleep, steps and recovery, provides additional "wins" that could keep them engaged, he stated.

Noom also plans to offer the wearable as something that members can "unlock" when they hit early milestones in the program, turning the hardware into an engagement incentive, executives said.

"We didn’t set out to build another wearable—we set out to build the ultimate metabolic health program that drives better health outcomes for members, leading to increased ROI for clients," Fair said.

"For employers and health intends, that’s the difference between a fitness perk that gets left in a drawer and a tool built to deliver health outcomes they’re already paying for and that is available to their population at no additional cost, he said.

Expensive wearables can undermine the ROI payers are looking for, Cook noted. "I essentially believe that the devices are a commodity and should effectively be given away. That’s why we're including the wearable at no additional cost to the payer," he mentioned.

According to recent reports, payers and employers also want to see ROI on health programs within a shorter time frame, within 12 to 24 months, Fair added. Providing employers with a program that combines behavior change, wearables and biomarker testing also reduces the number of vendors they have to work with, he added.

Health prepares want evidence that daily behavior changes translate into measurable clinical and financial outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure and A1C, and Noom plans to study whether its wearable can help deliver that ROI over the next year, Fair remarked.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ ACCESS Model could serve as a proving ground for Noom to demonstrate how the combination of its behavior change program with wearables such as the Noom Band can affect cardiometabolic health.

Noom looks to participate in CMS’ Advancing Chronic Care with Effective Scalable Solutions model under the cardio-kidney-metabolic clinical track, focusing on conditions like obesity, prediabetes and diabetes improvement. ACCESS is a 10-year initiative to integrate tech-enabled care into Medicare.

"That model is an outcomes-aligned payment model. We're excited to bundle the blood pressure cuff, the wearable, along with the Noom program, to have the absolute maximum effect on the outcomes that are being measured, outcomes like A1C, blood pressure and weight," Cook noted.

Cook is bullish that wearables will play a bigger role in chronic condition management as sensors are able to generate more sophisticated physiological data and AI gets better at interpreting the data.

"It should be possible, in my view, within years and maybe quicker than that to have the wearable signal itself provide a blood pressure signal that is validated, which would certainly simplify models like the CMS ACCESS model, if you didn't also have to ship a blood pressure cuff," he said. "These less invasive wearables, as they get more powerful, I think, can be transformative to healthcare generally, and I think the CMS ACCESS model is pointing the way to how they would democratize that, and at a relatively low cost to the ultimate payer.".

That means you want strong outsoles with responsive tread patterns and a midsole structure that can handle fast-twitch lateral movements. Pickleball shoes need to provide support, so buying the lightest shoe possible is not the smartest move. When buying a lightweight shoe (say, under 10 ounces) there's likely to be some sacrifice in support or stability. The trick? Stick to pickleball-specific shoes first. You can also consider tennis shoes and cross-trainers due to their similar support-first construction. Avoid featherlight running shoes that are built for a different type of movement.

Sources indicate that mesh is the most common and best material to look for in the upper of a pickleball shoe. However, like weight, you don't necessarily need the most breathable mesh possible. Some pickleball shoes sacrifice breathability to boost abrasion resistance, and to help keep your foot secure (like limiting your foot rolling and turning inside the shoe).

According to recent reports, when it comes to the outsole, look for a shoe that has a strong rubber pattern that will help grip surfaces and reduce the odds of slipping when turning your feet. Some pickleball shoes pay greater attention to tread pattern, which can help provide a feeling of better grip on a court. Outsole will largely come down to personal preference, as most are constructed about the same.

When looking at the midsole, aim for a shoe that has supportive cushioning (like EVA foam) and keeps a relatively low profile. Prioritizing a midsole with too much cushioning could lead you to a shoe that sits high (like a Hoka running shoe), thus leading to a less responsive design, which could potentially lead to a greater chance of rolling an ankle when making fast turns on the court.

I have been fortunate enough to rock quite a few pairs of pickleball shoes over the past few years. Having played on multiple surfaces, I’ve learned a few things about what to look for when selecting a pair. I also partnered with our other writers and editors at Men's Health to help select the best pickleball shoes we’ve tested in the past few years, available. We’ve compiled a guide to the best all-day play, taking great note of each shoe's stability, durability, weight, and price point. Special consideration was taken into account for pickleball shoes that had excellent traction and stability since those two qualities are the most key in a pickleball shoe.

Sources indicate that there is a lot of crossover from effective tennis shoes to pickleball shoes. So we also spoke to experts like Life Time Galleria Tennis Leader Gary Armstrong (who has been playing tennis for 36 years and has been an instructor for 17 years) and Life Time Charlotte Tennis Leader Eric Winn (who has been a tennis coach for 24 years and still plays in the 5.0 USTA leagues) to get their takes on the best tennis shoes for men. With minimal differences, some of their picks made it to this guide.

If you're someone who's going to play pickleball once or twice for recreation, then you could get away with a low-profile running shoe. But if you're expecting to play any more than that, we strongly recommend buying a proper pair of pickleball shoes.

Industry observers note that the reason we don't recommend wearing just any type of running shoe is that running shoes are made for forward motion, so there's often less emphasis on reinforcing the shoe for side-to-side movements. Running shoes also have less structure and stability than what you want in a pickleball shoe, as the running styles these days are made to be as lightweight and breathable as possible (with high cushioned stacks), which means less focus on overall support.

Recent findings suggest that so, to be clear, you should steer from wearing running shoes for pickleball if you expect to play the game on a regular basis. A proper pickleball shoe is a smart investment that will help give you traction and stability while greatly decreasing the chance of rolling an ankle or spraining a knee.

Engaging Medicaid’s Hardest-to-Reach Members Helps Plans Control Medical Spend" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Every Medicaid managed care initiative has them.They’re the members who remain outside the reach of traditional outreach and care management after the calls, texts, letters and emails haven’t worked. Their phone numbers may be disconnected, their addresses outdated. They’ve been targeted with different outreach strategies, even assigned to outside vendors that specialize in finding hard-to-reach members—and still remain disconnected.And they’re often among the members aims most need to reach.They’re Medicaid’s hardest-to-find, hardest-to-engage members: people with complex medical and behavioral health needs, often compounded by unstable housing, food insecurity, transportation barriers and other circumstances that make navigating healthcare extraordinarily difficult. Many are also among a plan’s highest-cost members, cycling through emergency departments and hospitals while remaining disconnected from care that could help stabilize their health.Plans have struggled for years to reach this population. What makes the challenge more urgent today is growing financial pressure on Medicaid plans to manage costs and demonstrate that every public healthcare dollar is yielding measurable results — and the recognition that some of the greatest opportunities to reduce avoidable spending and improve quality lies with high-risk, high-cost members traditional approaches still aren’t reaching.An estimated 4–8% of a managed healthcare plan’s Medicaid membership may fall into this hardest-to-engage cohort, driving an estimated 35-50% of an MCO’s total medical spend. he opportunity is to reach members who have remained disconnected and reduce the costly utilization that can occur when successful engagement never happens.When Traditional Outreach Has Run Its CourseManaged healthcare plans have built sophisticated outreach and care-management capabilities across multiple channels, supported by digital tools, data analytics and centralized teams. Many have changed tactics and brought in outside vendors. Those approaches work for most members.But the hardest-to-reach members are still left behind.For this population, simply finding the member is often the biggest challenge. Someone moving between temporary housing, shelters, encampments or other locations may be impossible to locate using the information a plan has on file. Finding that person may require combining data and technology with local knowledge, community relationships and people on the ground.And finding the member is only the beginning.A member may not trust the person who finds them. Housing, food, transportation or an immediate behavioral health need may matter far more at that moment than making a primary care appointment. Language differences and difficult experiences with the healthcare system can create additional barriers.That’s why the distinction between contact and engagement matters. Contact means reaching someone. Engagement means listening, building trust, addressing barriers and helping the member take the next step.What It Takes to Truly Engage MembersTechnology can help determine where to look, prioritize the next best action and make field teams more efficient. But technology doesn’t create trust. This is ultimately a human effort—technology-enabled but led by people.

Recent findings suggest that while finding members is often the hardest part, it’s only the beginning. What happens next is what can change outcomes.Experience with hardest-to-reach Medicaid populations has shown 25–40% reductions in ED utilization and 35–55% reductions in inpatient utilization after members were located and engaged, barriers addressed, and ongoing follow-through provided.*For intends, that’s where the financial opportunity lies. Reaching high-risk, high-cost members and helping them reconnect to care creates an opportunity to reduce avoidable ED visits and hospitalizations—and the costs that come with them.At a time when every avoidable ED visit and hospitalization matters, reaching and serving these members is more crucial than ever. It’s an opportunity to improve care while addressing a significant source of avoidable healthcare spending.

With cold weather already settling in, A-listers and influencers who call Fresh York City home are heading north to Beacon and the Catskills—turning these upstate towns into the ultimate winter hotspots.

Celebrities and influencers have have been heading over to for an upstate Latest York escape in winter's hotspots—and their appeal is easy to picture as the cold weather approaches.

Between Beacon’s waterfall-side boutique hotel and the Catskills’ mountain lodges with private soaking tubs, the destinations offer plenty of reasons to leave the city behind for a few days. For some visitors, a weekend away becomes the inspiration for something more permanent.

But what does it cost to buy a place in these coveted retreats, and how much attention are they attracting from New York home shoppers?

The Catskills have drawn Hollywood actors, reality stars, and influencers for vacations, weddings, and a quieter place to call home.

Olivia Wilde and Rami Malek have both stayed at a mountain lodge in Hunter. Jennifer Grey, Ali Wentworth, Olivia Rodrigo, and George Stephanopoulos also headed to the region in 2024 to celebrate the wedding of Schuyler Fox, the daughter of Michael J. Fox and Tracy Pollan.

That same summer, YouTube star Ethan Dolan and influencer Kristina Alice chose the Catskills for their own wedding. Alice later shared photographs from the celebration on Instagram, giving followers a glimpse of their romantic setting.

The fashion crowd has embraced the area, too. Vogue editor Naomi Elizée and Anthony Blue Jr. married in a meadow in Tannersville after welcoming guests for a weekend of festivities.

According to recent reports, for Amanda Seyfried, the Catskills offered a place to put down roots. The actress purchased a 1930s farm in 2013 while looking for a retreat from Hollywood, and the property became her main residence.

It has been revealed that across the Hudson, Beacon draws visitors with contemporary art, vintage shops, and an easy trip from Newly introduced York City. Model and creator Bri Scalesse documented a visit that included Dia Beacon and vintage shopping—an itinerary that works for a day trip or a longer weekend.

It has been revealed that according to Realtor.com® data, the median asking price in Beacon was $700,000 in September 2026. In Woodstock, a town included in the Catskills analysis, the median asking price was $968,750 in October.

Industry observers note that those figures offer snapshots of two individual markets. The broader home-search analysis covers all of Dutchess County, where Beacon is located, and five Catskills counties.

According to Realtor.com data, the Catskills accounted for 1.17% of all listing views from the New York City metro in the third quarter of 2026, up from 1.03% a year earlier.

Dutchess County’s share rose from 0.53% to 0.58%, giving the Catskills roughly twice its share of NYC-area browsing.

Both destinations gained a bigger share of a shrinking pool of views. NYC-metro views of Catskills listings fell about 28% year over year, while views of Dutchess County listings declined about 31%. NYC-area views across all listings fell more sharply, by about 37%.

It has been revealed that latest York remained the largest source of listing views for both destinations, even as shoppers elsewhere accounted for more of their audience. NYC-metro shoppers generated 37.5% of Catskills listing views, down from 42.3% a year earlier. In Dutchess County, their share slipped from 43.3% to 39.8%.

“Winter getaway buzz hasn’t translated into a winter surge in home shopping,” claims Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

Sources indicate that “Interest in the Catskills and Beacon follows normal seasonal patterns, but both places hold on to the attention of Latest York–area shoppers better than most markets, and they’re taking up a growing share of what those shoppers look at. At the same time, New York–area shoppers make up a smaller share of the audience for each destination than they did a year ago.”.

According to Realtor.com data, NYC-metro listing views fell 21% to 25% in the Catskills and 19% to 25% in Dutchess County between the third and fourth quarters over the three years analyzed. Those declines were broadly in line with the national seasonal slowdown.

Sources indicate that NYC-area views across all listings fell more sharply, by 30% to 37%, allowing both destinations to capture a larger share of attention heading into the holidays. In 2025, for example, the Catskills’ share of NYC-metro browsing rose from 1.03% in the third quarter to 1.23% in the fourth.

Industry observers note that from the fourth quarter to the first, NYC-metro views fell by 2%, 8%, and 15% in the Catskills and by 6%, 5%, and 16% in Dutchess County across the three winters studied. Over those same periods, NYC-metro views across all listings rose by 2% to 10%.

For buyers picturing a winter retreat, the figures show that home browsing in these destinations slows after the holidays, even as Newly introduced Yorkers’ searches pick up elsewhere.

#6359. Cancer uses antioxidants to disarm the immune system, scientists discover

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1195 w)
📖 Baca

Cancer uses antioxidants to disarm the immune system, scientists discover

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, free radicals have traditionally been associated with damage to the body's cells, leading to widespread interest in whether antioxidants might help prevent cancer.
  • Scientists have discovered that certain immune cells actually need small amounts of reactive oxygen species, a group of molecules that includes free radicals, to recognize and destroy cancer cells.
  • In a recent development, the findings, published in the journal Science, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer evades the body's defenses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, free radicals have traditionally been associated with damage to the body's cells, leading to widespread interest in whether antioxidants might help prevent cancer. But new research suggests these often misunderstood molecules also play an important role in protecting us from the disease.

Scientists have discovered that certain immune cells actually need small amounts of reactive oxygen species, a group of molecules that includes free radicals, to recognize and destroy cancer cells. Even more surprisingly, tumors appear to exploit this requirement by releasing natural antioxidants that interfere with the immune system's ability to fight back.

In a recent development, the findings, published in the journal Science, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer evades the body's defenses. They could also point toward new strategies for making cancer immunotherapies more effective, particularly in patients whose tumors resist existing treatments.

How Cancer Uses Antioxidants to Disable Immune Cells.

The immune system protects the body by identifying and eliminating threats, ranging from harmful bacteria and viruses to abnormal cells that can develop into cancer. Among its most key defenses are specialized immune cells called T cells, which can recognize and destroy tumor cells.

In a recent development, however, these cancer-fighting cells depend on chemical signals to activate their destructive abilities. Small amounts of reactive oxygen species provide some of those signals, helping T cells switch into attack mode.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom and Oregon Health & Science University in the United States discovered that tumors can interfere with this process. By examining the fluid surrounding cells inside tumors grown in mice, they found that cancer cells create chemical conditions that effectively prevent nearby T cells from activating.

According to recent reports, the key is a naturally occurring antioxidant protein called Peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1). Cancer cells release large quantities of this protein into their surroundings, where it removes the reactive oxygen species that T cells need to function. Without those activating signals, the immune cells become less effective at destroying cancer.

In effect, tumors use antioxidants as a chemical shield, weakening the immune response that would otherwise threaten their survival.

Removing Cancer's Antioxidant Shield Slows Tumor Growth.

To investigate whether this defense mechanism could be disrupted, the researchers used CRISPR gene editing to modify cancer cells in mice. The edited cells could no longer produce PRDX1, allowing the team to examine what happened when tumors lost their ability to release the antioxidant protein.

The results were encouraging. Without PRDX1, immune cells became more active, and tumor growth was reduced. This suggested that interfering with the antioxidant protein could restore some of the immune system's ability to attack cancer.

Sources indicate that the researchers then investigated whether human cancers use the same strategy. They examined existing data on proteins released by human cancer cell lines, studied patterns of gene activity in thousands of human tumors, and analyzed fluid collected from tumors surgically removed from patients.

In a recent development, all three lines of evidence supported the same conclusion. Human cancers also release PRDX1 into the surrounding environment, where it can eliminate the reactive oxygen species that cancer-fighting T cells rely on.

It has been revealed that dr. Xan Wesolowski, one of the lead authors from the University of Cambridge's Department of Pathology, explained why the discovery challenges conventional thinking about these molecules.

In a recent development, "We tend to think of reactive oxygen species purely as damaging byproducts of metabolism. But we are increasingly understanding they have notable functions within cells, and T cells need them to activate. Our study develops this picture, revealing that tumors can exploit this very dependency to evade elimination.".

A New Strategy for Making Cancer Immunotherapy More Effective.

Recent findings suggest that cancer treatment has increasingly focused on helping the immune system recognize and eliminate malignant cells. These approaches, known as immunotherapies, have produced remarkable results for some patients, but many others experience little or no benefit.

Sources indicate that the fresh research identifies a possible reason certain tumors can withstand immune attacks. By releasing PRDX1, cancer cells may suppress the very T cells that immunotherapies are designed to activate.

It has been revealed that importantly, the researchers found that preventing cancer cells from producing this antioxidant improved their response to immunotherapy in experimental models. Some tumors that had previously resisted treatment became responsive when the antioxidant defense was disrupted.

Professor Rahul Roychoudhuri, also from Cambridge's Department of Pathology, mentioned the findings identify a promising target for future cancer treatments.

According to recent reports, "We've found a upcoming way by which cancers shut down the immune system. When we block this process, tumors that don't respond to some immunotherapies start responding to treatment. That tells us this is a pathway worth targeting therapeutically, and there are several ways we might be able to achieve this.".

The discovery also raises the possibility of using a different type of chemical approach to strengthen the immune response.

Dr. Robert Eil from the School of Medicine at Oregon Health & Science University remarked: "Our study suggests a possible way to boost T cell immunotherapies. Rather than using antioxidants, it could be that prooxidants can kickstart the T cells into action against tumor cells.".

Why the Findings Raise Questions About Antioxidant Supplements.

Beyond their potential implications for cancer treatment, the results may help explain a longstanding puzzle involving antioxidant supplements.

Recent findings suggest that antioxidants have frequently been promoted for their ability to neutralize reactive oxygen species and protect cells from damage. Because these molecules can contribute to processes associated with cancer development, researchers have investigated whether taking antioxidant supplements might reduce cancer risk.

Industry observers note that however, several large randomized clinical trials have failed to demonstrate such protection. In some cases, antioxidant supplementation has even been associated with worse outcomes.

Sources indicate that the latest findings suggest one possible explanation. Although reactive oxygen species can damage cells, they also help activate the immune defenses that fight cancer. Removing too many of these molecules could unintentionally interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize and destroy tumors.

This does not establish that antioxidant supplements generally promote cancer, but it highlights the importance of understanding how these molecules behave in different biological settings.

The researchers also emphasize that their experimental findings remain preclinical. Although they identified evidence of the same antioxidant mechanism in human cancers, the potential treatment strategies have not yet been established as safe or effective in patients.

People living with cancer should therefore not change their diets, supplement use, or medical treatments based on these findings without consulting a healthcare professional.

The research was largely supported by the Medical Research Council, the European Research Council, Wellcome, and the National Institutes of Health/National Cancer Institute.

These healthcare systems were designed before modern artificial intelligence existed, so AI arrives as a separate vendor, a separate login, and a separate integration project. Unlike most hospital EHRs, the eClinicalWorks® AI-native inpatient hospital EHR was designed with a different approach: leveraging AI and automation to reduce administrative burden, streamline operational workflows, and improve efficiency without increasing technology complexity or cost.Reimagining the Hospital TechnologyThe eClinicalWorks AI-native inpatient hospital EHR supports hospital staff across every department, helping to streamline documentation, retrieve clinical records at the point of care, enhance billing, and automate routine tasks, all while keeping healthcare professionals in control of final decisions. It leverages the new eClinicalWorks Smart Canvas, a redesigned workspace where consumers can access relevant information, tasks, and actions through a more intuitive interface.Alabama-based Lakeland Community Hospital selected the eClinicalWorks inpatient hospital EHR. Wes Sigler, MPA, CFO/COO at the hospital, expressed that "It's going to not only improve our experience on the clinical side but also make our experience on the hospital side even more amazing." The new workspace helps clinicians and staff complete routine tasks and review relevant information seamlessly. Fully integrated AI capabilities across the unified platform further support hospital operations:.

Recent findings suggest that AI Agents as Force MultipliersThe next phase of healthcare focuses on creating operationally intelligent healthcare environments. The eClinicalWorks AI Workbench enables organizations to build, customize, and deploy AI agents that automate routine tasks, improve efficiency, and reduce administrative burdens for hospital staff and providers.Financial performance remains one of the largest challenges facing healthcare organizations. eClinicalWorks is extending AI-driven capabilities into areas such as autonomous revenue cycle management (RCM) and autonomous value-based care (VBC), helping organizations streamline financial, administrative, and care management processes while reducing manual effort.Extending Operational Intelligence to PharmacyModern pharmacy technology, such as the eClinicalWorks Pharmacy Management System, connects pharmacists, providers, and patients through a shared record, helping to eliminate communication silos and reduce duplicate work. This can help bring operational workflows into a single environment. Peyton Frye, COO at East Georgia Healthcare Center, collaborated closely with eClinicalWorks to develop the newly introduced pharmacy system. He shared how information such as patient contact details is now synchronized between the medical and pharmacy sides, eliminating the need to patch multiple systems. For hospitals, this creates a more connected experience across inpatient, ambulatory, and pharmacy workflows, helping teams access the information they need without having to navigate multiple systems or fragmented processes. When inpatient, ambulatory, and pharmacy workflows operate within a connected platform, hospitals can reduce duplication, eliminate unnecessary handoffs, and improve visibility across departments.Building the Future of Connected CareIn an era defined by mounting workforce challenges and financial pressures, the goal is not simply to add more technology. It is to build a smarter hospital environment where information, workflows, and AI work together to help organizations deliver high-quality care more efficiently.The next frontier is creating hospitals that can leverage AI to streamline operations, coordinate care, and support clinicians in real time.eClinicalWorks is advancing this vision with an AI-native hospital platform that connects inpatient, ambulatory, pharmacy, and revenue cycle workflows through a unified experience. By combining embedded AI, customizable agents, workflow automation, and a shared patient record, hospitals can reduce administrative burden while creating a more connected environment for both care teams and patients.
