  • A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible.
  • The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment.
  • Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. Newly introduced preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms.

The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.

In a recent development, "Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more promptly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness blueprint," Piwnica-Worms stated. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response.".

Why Radiation Therapy Can Damage the Intestines.

Radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure.

Recent findings suggest that when this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options.

Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory demonstrated that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect.

The latest study provides an vital piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury.

How a 24-Hour Fast Activates Gut Repair.

Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila, also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage.

Propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

In a recent development, these modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant.

In effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining.

One Gut Bacterium Proves Essential for Recovery.

Industry observers note that to determine how crucial AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits.

Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study.

In a recent development, the results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs.

According to recent reports, by uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential new way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment.

Could Gut Bacteria Make Cancer Treatment Safer?

Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy.

According to recent reports, one possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage.

If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy.

Sources indicate that importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care.

Industry observers note that "Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai noted. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need.".

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT).

#6351. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. Latest research indicates otherwise

For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. Latest research indicates otherwise

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight.
  • A latest Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence.
  • Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several notable nutrients.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

A latest Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several notable nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise upcoming questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

Why Full-Fat Dairy Has Been Discouraged.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Sources indicate that often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

In a recent development, participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

The results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

Industry observers note that the higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," claims Anderson.

Blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

The Surprising Science Behind Dairy Fat.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," states Anderson.

Casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how quickly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

The broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Vital for Older Adults.

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

It has been revealed that as people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other important bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The latest findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients.

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

Recent findings suggest that traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

Sources indicate that that does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything.".

As a lifelong distance runner, I’ve had trouble finding low-impact cardio workouts that feel challenging enough when I’m not pounding the pavement. But that all changed when I discovered an exercise trampoline, also referred to as a rebounder. They use a similar style of trampoline to what you used to bounce around on as a kid in the backyard, just with a fitness twist. The result is that the sized-down versions are just as fun, but you also work up a sweat.

In a recent development, using an exercise trampoline is known as rebounding, and this type of workout is considered a high-intensity movement that’s low impact. That sounds a little confusing, but it basically means using an exercise trampoline will get your heart rate up there while giving your joints a break, something that can be especially appealing for runners. If you’re like me and crave a challenging lower-impact workout that doesn’t include an exercise bike or rower, rebounding might be your new favorite cardio workout.

In a recent development, while rebounding workouts will get your heart rate up promptly, there are plenty of other health benefits to consider, too. A 2024 scientific review found that rebounding can be great for enhancing blood circulation, bone health, and balance. And a small, 2018 study of 18 women found that participants were able to lower their blood pressure and improve their VO2 max—a marker of cardiovascular fitness—on a 12-week rebounding program.

Outside of research studies, Nikki Gnozzio, CPT lists off rebounding benefits of better balance, overall strength, and, of course, more fun. That last part is worth considering, especially if you’ve been struggling with workout motivation or boredom.

Of course, you need a trampoline before you can try this out. According to the personal trainers we spoke with, a rebounder’s tension, adjustability, maximum weight, sturdiness, and size should all factor into your buying decision. Below are six options that stood out.

There are a lot of brands to choose from, but JumpSport stands out as one that’s stood the test of time. “JumpSport has been around since 1996 and is a well-respected brand,” states Melissa Cantillo, an ACE-certified personal trainer and fitness manager at Canyon Ranch. The brand’s mini trampoline line, which includes the JumpSport 530 Pro, popularized the bungee cord system that’s used in many exercise trampolines, she points out.

Industry observers note that this trampoline uses 36 adjustable elastic cords for a quieter bounce, with seven firmness settings to help you find your ideal tension. It also uses 16-gauge steel tubing for durability, which is why you can use this trampoline inside or outside (just make sure you bring it back indoors after a good bouncing session to extend the life of your trampoline).

It has been revealed that the JumpSport 530 Pro has an extension skirt to protect your feet in case you accidentally land on the cords. The legs are slightly arched at the top to lower the risk your trampoline will tip over. If space is a premium at your place, simply remove the legs and stash your trampoline in a closet or up against a wall to free up floor space.

Read more: Best Under-Desk Treadmills.

It has been revealed that plenty of trampolines have features to help you break them down into a smaller size for storage. The Skybound Boogie Bounce Elite takes that even further, with a trampoline that folds in half like a taco and slides into an included carrying bag. The trampoline is relatively small to begin with—it has a 39-inch diameter—but that works in your favor when it comes to storage.

There’s a lot more to love about this trampoline, though. It has a built-in, adjustable handlebar for balance, which is especially handy given that smaller bouncing surface. The frame and skirt are already installed once it arrives, so you can simply snap in the legs and handlebar to get bouncing within minutes.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for workout guidance, you’ll appreciate the free one-month trial of the Boogie Bounce app. It shares more than 100 routines you can flip through. After that, it’s $4.99 a month.

Read More: Best Pilates Reformer Machine.

The Stamina 36-inch Mini Trampoline has a petite enough size that won’t hog your workout space. It’s also just over $50, making it the most affordable option in our guide.

In addition to its smaller circumference, it has detachable rubber legs you can pop out to prop against a wall or slide under your bed. Taylor Beebe, CPT points out that the weight capacity is also a bit lower than the other models—250 pounds—but the whole thing collapses for convenience. She also praises the included Müüv app that offers trampoline workouts.This trampoline uses resistance bands instead of steel coils, which likely contributes to its lower weight limit. So, if you weigh more than 250 pounds, it’s best to look for a different model, like the Leaps & Bounds Rebounder. It also doesn’t have a handlebar for added stability, although the 49.5-inch model does.

Many fitness trampolines have removable legs, but some are easier to get on and off than others. While some require some serious muscle and maneuvering to get these in and out, the Leaps & Bounds Bungee Rebounder has legs that just screw into the bottom, creating a pretty flat, easy-to-store surface when you’re ready to stash it away.

In a recent development, this trampoline comes in your choice of 40- and 48-inch diameters. (This is the 40-inch model, but you can upgrade to the 48-inch option if you have the room for it.) The Bungee Rebounder uses adjustable elastic cords for quiet bouncing, along with a durable carbon steel frame.

It has been revealed that leaps & Bounds offers rare perks you won’t see with most other exercise trampoline brands: You can return this after 30 days if it’s not a good fit, and the trampoline comes with a lifetime warranty. While this is minor, it’s still worth mentioning: This trampoline comes in your choice of seven cord colors. Just be aware that if you want to tack on a stability bar, it will set you back an extra $93.

Recent findings suggest that exercise trampolines generally fall into a category known as rebounders or “mini trampolines,” which basically means they’re smaller than those massive ones kids use in backyards. But rebounders have a relatively small bouncing surface, so you have to be a little mindful about where you jump. The ACON Fit Hexagon Rebounder is 55 inches across, with a 40-inch bouncing surface, which is one of the largest you’ll find. That’s worth considering, whether you prefer a larger bouncing area or just want to build in some added insurance that you won’t accidentally rebound off.

This trampoline has a built-in handlebar that’s adjustable, in case you want extra help with balancing while you jump. The reinforced steel frame has six arched legs for stability. Keep in mind that the legs aren’t removable, just in case you want to store your trampoline in a closet or other smaller space.

The elastic cords allow for a quieter bouncing experience. (The trampoline comes with extra bungees in case one breaks.) This trampoline comes with a 10-year warranty on the frame and two-year coverage on the mat to help protect your investment.

The Sunny Health Springless trampoline delivers the basics at a relatively moderate price tag, making it ideal for those fresh to rebounding and still figuring out if it’s for them.

This trampoline has a less common square shape, which tends to provide a more consistent, uniform bounce across the entire mat. Since this trampoline is on the smaller side, that’s especially handy for small spaces. The smaller size and removable legs mean it won’t hog a lot of room at your place.

Another perk for beginners? The Sunny Health Springless comes with the free SunnyFit app, which includes rebounding workouts to get you started.

Tension is the tightness and level of resistance you’ll have on the trampoline as you jump. “Smaller exercise trampolines will be more resistant (have higher tension) because they sit closer to the ground, and you don’t want to be tapping the ground with each jump,” indicates Sydney Sherman, NASM-CPT. “They’re meant to absorb the shock as you land your jump, which is why they’re a great low-impact option for those of us with sensitive joints or coming back from an injury.".

Industry observers note that some trampolines allow you to tweak the settings to better suit your needs. An adjustable handle is key (if your trampoline has a handle), Gnozzio says. But some will also allow you to adjust the tension to create a bouncier or less bouncy feeling.

The maximum weight limit for an exercise trampoline will be different based on how it is constructed or the brand. Generally, the weight limit often varies from 250 to 450 pounds. The sturdiness of an exercise trampoline will also vary, but you'll want to make sure it has rubber grip covers for the legs to stay in place (and not scrape your floors) and a handlebar that doesn't easily move for stability.

Sure, you’re already aware that your trampoline needs to fit in your room. But you need plenty of room around it, like a foot on either side, just to be safe. "A lot of trampoline workouts involve arm movements, so you’ll want to have space around you, as well as above you for jumping," claims Gnozzio.

While you’re at it, don’t forget to factor in your ceiling height. A minimum 8-foot ceiling height is recommended, according to Cantillo. You don’t need to bounce in a room with an extra-high ceiling since you push into the trampoline more than you jump up, she explains. “Your feet may come off the trampoline anywhere from 1 inch to 8 inches depending on the workout,” Cantillo indicates.

When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why.
  • Plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health.
  • Industry observers note that fiber is particularly key because it provides food for gut microbes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why. New research suggests that fiber is only part of the story. Certain plant proteins that resist digestion may also play a surprisingly important role in shaping gut bacteria and determining whether they produce beneficial or potentially harmful substances.

Plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health. One reason is that they help maintain a diverse community of microorganisms in the intestines, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Many of these bacteria are beneficial, helping break down food components that the human digestive system cannot process on its own.

Industry observers note that fiber is particularly key because it provides food for gut microbes. Plants also contain phytochemicals, natural substances that often give fruits and vegetables their vibrant colors and help protect them from environmental threats. These compounds can also contribute to human health. Yet researchers have only begun to understand the complicated chemical interactions that occur when gut bacteria digest plant foods.

According to recent reports, two studies led by Jenna AbuSalim and Joshua Rabinowitz, director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, provide notable new insights. One, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, shows how plant fiber and certain proteins influence gut bacteria to favor the production of beneficial compounds over potentially harmful ones. The other, published in Nature Metabolism in June, challenges the longstanding belief that many important chemical compounds circulating in the body originate exclusively from intestinal microbes.

Sources indicate that "There's growing interest across medical disciplines in manipulating the human microbiome or using its metabolic products themselves for therapy," said Rabinowitz. "Diet holds great promise for controlling the microbiome and its outputs. But to devise effective therapeutic interventions, we need to understand what aspects of the diet control which microbial outputs.".

How Plant Foods Change the Chemicals Your Gut Produces.

In the PNAS study, researchers examined a group of substances called phenol metabolites. Metabolites are chemicals formed when the body or microorganisms break down and process nutrients. Some are essential for normal biological functions, while others can contribute to health problems when they accumulate.

The phenol metabolites investigated by the team are produced when gut bacteria process two amino acids, tyrosine and phenylalanine. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, but the compounds they ultimately produce can have very different effects on health.

Two metabolites derived from phenylalanine, phenylpropionate and hippuric acid, are associated with healthy body weight and better gut health. In contrast, two compounds derived from tyrosine, p-cresol sulfate and phenol sulfate, have been linked to worse outcomes in cancer patients and harmful effects throughout the body in people with kidney disease.

The researchers wanted to understand whether different components of plant foods could influence which of these substances gut microbes produce.

"Our studies demonstrated that both the fiber and indigestible proteins from plants -- which we call 'proteins imitating fiber,' or Prif -- shift the balance of phenol metabolites from the harmful kind made from tyrosine to the healthful variety derived from phenylalanine," stated AbuSalim.

An Overlooked Plant Protein Works Alongside Fiber.

Although the health benefits of dietary fiber have been studied extensively, scientists have paid much less attention to plant proteins that pass through the digestive system without being fully broken down.

In a recent development, the researchers found that these indigestible proteins, which they call Prif, can reach the gut microbiome and serve as material for bacterial metabolism. In doing so, they influence which microbes thrive and which chemical compounds are produced.

Sources indicate that importantly, these proteins do not work in isolation. They cooperate with plant fiber to change how gut bacteria process nutrients, shifting their activity toward the production of beneficial phenol metabolites.

This discovery suggests that the nutritional value of plant foods may depend on more than their familiar concentrations of fiber, vitamins, and minerals. The amount and type of protein that escapes digestion could also help determine how food influences the gut microbiome.

When Gut Bacteria Run Low on Fiber, They May Feed on Your Gut's Protective Mucus.

One of the most intriguing findings concerns where gut bacteria obtain the raw materials used to produce harmful metabolites.

To investigate, the researchers labeled proteins with stable (non-radioactive) isotopes, allowing them to track exactly where the proteins traveled and how they were processed in the digestive systems of mice. This technique works by giving molecules a detectable chemical signature without making them radioactive.

The experiments revealed an important difference between the sources of beneficial and harmful phenols.

Sources indicate that the potentially harmful phenols came from gut bacteria breaking down proteins belonging to the host, including proteins found in the mucus layer that coats the intestines. This protective mucus helps separate intestinal microbes from the cells lining the gut and forms part of the body's natural defenses.

Meanwhile, the beneficial phenols were produced almost entirely from indigestible proteins supplied by food.

Industry observers note that fiber helped suppress the bacterial breakdown of the gut's protective mucus, reducing the production of harmful phenols. The indigestible plant proteins (Prif), in turn, supplied more dietary protein to gut bacteria, encouraging them to produce beneficial compounds instead.

Industry observers note that together, the findings reveal two complementary ways plant foods can influence intestinal chemistry. Fiber helps discourage bacteria from consuming proteins in the gut's protective mucus, while Prif provides an alternative source of nutrients that supports the production of healthier metabolites.

"We think Prifs represent an emerging class of dietary nutrients that shape the composition of the gut microbiome and could have a far-reaching influence on metabolic health," mentioned AbuSalim.

The implications could eventually extend to nutrition labels and dietary recommendations.

"Food packaging may eventually list Prif right below fiber," remarked Rabinowitz.

A Second Discovery Challenges What Scientists Thought About Gut Bacteria.

The companion study in Nature Metabolism addressed another important question: Are gut bacteria really responsible for producing all the metabolites traditionally attributed to them?

Along with phenol metabolites, the researchers examined indole metabolites, which are formed from tryptophan, another amino acid found in dietary proteins.

According to recent reports, these substances have attracted considerable scientific interest because they participate in biological processes linked to inflammation, immune activity, and disease. Researchers have investigated their involvement in inflammatory bowel disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and cancer. Some indole metabolites have also been found to influence the spread of cancer and the immune system's ability to attack tumors.

Scientists have generally assumed that gut bacteria are the source of these compounds. That belief has encouraged efforts to develop probiotics and dietary interventions that increase the production of potentially beneficial indole metabolites.

However, this approach depends on an important assumption: that intestinal microbes are responsible for producing most or all of the compounds researchers want to influence.

If the body's own cells make substantial amounts of these metabolites, changing the microbiome may not be the most effective way to control their levels.

Your Body Can Make Compounds Once Attributed to Gut Microbes.

To investigate, the research team used isotope tracing in mice, rats, and human cells to follow how different metabolites were produced.

The results challenged conventional thinking. Mammalian cells were capable of generating numerous phenol and indole metabolites independently of intestinal bacteria.

Among these were indole-3-lactate and indole-3-acetate, two biologically vital compounds previously considered products of microbial metabolism.

The researchers also examined what happened when antibiotics disrupted the intestinal microbiome. If certain metabolites depended entirely on gut bacteria, their concentrations would be expected to decline sharply when those bacteria were depleted.

According to recent reports, but many metabolites remained at substantial levels in the blood of antibiotic-treated mice. A similar pattern appeared in samples from patients receiving antibiotics, including people undergoing cancer treatment.

Other compounds behaved differently. Levels of indole-3-propionate and p-cresol sulfate, which are produced exclusively by microbes, declined following antibiotic treatment.

These results provided further evidence that some metabolites depend on intestinal bacteria, while others can also be manufactured by the body's own metabolic processes.

The distinction matters because it could change how researchers develop treatments intended to increase beneficial metabolites or reduce harmful ones.

What These Discoveries Mean for Nutrition and Future Treatments.

Together, the two studies offer a more detailed understanding of how diet, gut microbes, and the body's own metabolism interact.

The first identifies an overlooked category of plant proteins that works with fiber to influence bacterial activity, potentially helping shift the balance away from harmful metabolic products. The second demonstrates that the body itself can produce many compounds once believed to originate exclusively from gut bacteria.

Both findings have implications for research into metabolic disease, digestive health, cancer, and other conditions involving the microbiome.

They also suggest that attempts to manipulate gut chemistry through diet, probiotics, or other therapies will need to account for both microbial activity and the body's own metabolic capabilities.

Much of the experimental evidence comes from animals and laboratory studies, so additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms influence long-term health outcomes in people.

Nevertheless, a better understanding of the relationship between different food components and microbial metabolism could eventually make dietary advice more precise and help researchers identify fresh therapeutic strategies.

"Beyond that," stated Rabinowitz, "a clearer picture of how different foods interact with the microbiome to modulate the production of bacterial metabolites will help sharpen the guidance nutritionists and doctors can give to people for disease prevention and therapy.".

These studies were funded by the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, the National Institutes of Health, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the Princeton Alliance for Collaborative Research and Innovation, Princeton University.

Aside from his post as Director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Joshua Rabinowitz is Professor in the Department of Chemistry & Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics and a member of the Rutgers Cancer Institute.

Ambient clinical intelligence platform Suki announced Monday the launch of an agentic operating system designed to connect fragmented healthcare technology.

Recent findings suggest that the operating system—dubbed Suki OS—is built on three core pillars, the tech giant notes: a partner ecosystem, unified artificial intelligence agents and a performance guarantee. It aims to expand the capabilities beyond its Suki for Clinicians platform over time.

Suki is introducing two initial AI agent initiatives as part of its goal to reduce administrative work.

According to recent reports, suki Prior Authorization will streamline the process by identifying requirements and gathering supporting clinical documentation. Its Clinical Documentation Improvement (CDI) Agent will focus on identifying documentation gaps, improving accuracy and supporting downstream coding and revenue cycle workflows.

Additional agents are planned across clinical, operational and financial workflows as part of the tech giant’s broader strategy to develop agents that can execute complex workflows with human oversight.

Suki’s Partner Ecosystem is comprised of its Insight Partners, which integrate intelligence with Suki patient context, and Platform Partners, which let health tech companies embed Suki’s AI directly into their products.

The Suki Guarantee offers eligible customers up to a 100% refund if agreed-upon performance targets aren't met, the company says.

Suki CEO and Founder Punit Soni told Fierce Healthcare that healthcare has an "execution problem" rather than an AI shortage.

In a recent development, "We've spent years building technology that can understand clinical conversations, but understanding is only the beginning," Soni noted. "The real opportunity is to turn that intelligence into action, connecting the systems, people and workflows that make healthcare run.".

That’s the motivation behind Suki OS, according to Soni.

Recent findings suggest that "Nearly a decade ago, we pioneered ambient AI, and today, our technology is trusted by more than 450 healthcare organizations, with independently validated clinical and financial outcomes," Soni mentioned. "We've built deep clinical intelligence, integrations across EHRs, and an expansive partner ecosystem. That foundation uniquely positions Suki to move beyond documentation and help automate the complex work that surrounds patient care.".

Industry observers note that soni remarked that the next generation of AI tools have to "do more than save time" as health systems face mounting financial pressures and workforce constraints. "It has to deliver meaningful clinical and financial outcomes," he said.

Sources indicate that soni continued, "Ultimately, the measure of AI's success won't be how many agents we build. It will be how much complexity we remove from healthcare, how much time we give back to clinicians and their patients, and how much measurable financial value we create for the organizations delivering care.".

In October, the firm secured $90 million in series E funding to accelerate its growth and continue expanding its AI capabilities.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer has raised more than $250 million to date, executives say. Patient encounters supported by its tools grew more than 190% year over year in 2026, with revenue doubling in 2025 and on track for similar growth this year.

Why is crypto down? Bitcoin crashed below $69,000 just now, dragging the crypto markets into another brutal selloff. Ethereum slipped below $2,000, while several major altcoins recorded losses exceeding 6%.

According to recent reports, the decline comes as crypto faces a dangerous combination of shrinking dollar liquidity, institutional withdrawals, and aggressive leveraged selling. The situation is becoming increasingly uncomfortable. Investors are pulling capital from stablecoins and Bitcoin ETFs, leaving fewer buyers to absorb selling pressure. Once Bitcoin broke below $70,000, leveraged traders faced another wave of forced liquidations.

The biggest warning sign comes from the stablecoin market, where the amount of available dollar liquidity is shrinking rapidly. Glassnode reported that major stablecoin supply declined by $14.2 billion over 30 days. This is the sharpest decline since the 2022 bear market, when the Terra collapse triggered widespread capital withdrawals.

Total stablecoin supply has fallen below $280 billion, returning to levels last seen around September 2025. Meanwhile, CryptoQuant recorded a $6.6 billion decline in USDT market cap over 60 days through November 7. This is concerning because the USDT contraction exceeded twice the decline recorded following the FTX collapse in December 2022.

Stablecoins function as crypto’s cash reserves. Traders use USDT and USDC to move between exchanges, purchase crypto, and maintain liquidity without leaving the blockchain ecosystem. So, when investors redeem stablecoins for dollars, that purchasing power leaves the market. Glassnode itself warned that shrinking supply leaves less fuel available for another rally.

Sources indicate that the liquidity problem is arriving alongside persistent institutional selling. US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $1.6 billion across 20 trading sessions. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $47.7 million in net outflows on November 12, extending their withdrawal streak to six consecutive trading sessions.

It has been revealed that bitwise’s BITB led withdrawals with $26.4 million, while Morgan Stanley’s MSBT recorded $3.3 million in inflows. Ethereum ETFs also showed at least $8 million in net outflows in November 12 data.

It has been revealed that the combination creates an uncomfortable situation. Crypto is losing dollar liquidity while regulated investment products continue recording withdrawals. There are fewer fresh buyers available to support prices when sellers rush toward the exit.

The liquidity squeeze eventually reached the derivatives market, where falling prices triggered another wave of forced selling. Bitcoin plunged 7% over 24 hours to $68,400 in 15 minutes this morning. Ethereum dropped 6% to $1,920, while BNB declined 6.3% and XRP lost 3.5%.

Liquidations also hit $1.64 billion over 24 hours. Long positions accounted for $1.46 billion, with more than 175,000 traders losing their positions. The damage accelerated after Bitcoin lost the $70,000 level. Traders betting on a recovery suddenly faced liquidation thresholds, forcing exchanges to close leveraged positions.

It has been revealed that these forced closures created a feedback loop that pushed prices lower and exposed more leveraged positions. Macro conditions are not helping, too. Recent findings suggest that A stronger dollar and rising Treasury yields also weakened demand for speculative assets. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s leadership crisis unsettled technology markets, adding to the risk-off mood.

In a recent development, when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

According to recent reports, not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing newly introduced opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

In a recent development, with digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Industry observers note that even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

According to recent reports, the approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

In a recent development, another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

According to recent reports, REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Sources indicate that finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech tech giant could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

According to recent reports, investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years.   • Located at 185 Steele Street, with 37 private residences ranging from studios to penthouses, Waldorf Astoria Residences Cherry Creek is slated to open in early 2028.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Legendary hospitality brand Waldorf Astoria has chosen a neighborhood ten minutes from downtown Denver for its first foray into residential living in Colorado.

Located at 185 Steele Street, with 37 private residences ranging from studios to penthouses, Waldorf Astoria Residences Cherry Creek is slated to open in early 2028.

With architecture by SAR+, interiors by BAMO, and conceptual design by Carlos Ott, prices start at $1.5 million for a studio and cap out at $13 million for the largest penthouse.

While the luxury leader could have set down in a high-end ski haven like Aspen, Vail, or Telluride, the tech giant instead went with Cherry Creek, a dense, walkable retail corridor five miles from the center of Denver.

The neighborhood's median price per square foot is $293, according to Realtor.com data, compared to $334 for the overall Denver metropolitan area.

Featuring two major commercial destinations—Cherry Creek North and Cherry Creek Shopping Center—the global brand felt this was the place to make its residential debut in the Rocky Mountain state.

The brand's housing portfolio is set to nearly triple, reaching 34 properties and 3,498 units by 2030, according to the organization.

Recent findings suggest that residences are particularly clustered in Florida, with condo buildings in Pompano Beach, St. Petersburg, Sarasota, and Miami. Other locations include Newly introduced York City; Atlanta, GA; Chicago, IL; Las Vegas, NV; Park City, UT; and Maui, HI.

Cherry Creek, in a small, dense 16-block radius, may seem an unexpected choice to join in this world renowned group of cities, but the developer notes it as an easy decision.

"We recognized early on that Denver was ready for a world-class, branded luxury residential offering, and Cherry Creek was the natural fit," Ryan Shear, managing partner at developer Property Markets Group (PMG), told Realtor.com.

"The neighborhood’s established luxury market, vibrant retail and dining scene, and distinctive character aligned perfectly with the Waldorf Astoria brand and the kind of project we aimed to deliver.".

"Cherry Creek has long been one of Denver's most prestigious neighborhoods," Dawn Raymond of Kentwood Real Estate, who is heading up sales in the complex, tells Realtor.com.

She touts the district's central location, walkability, eye-catching architecture, high-end shopping options, art galleries, and a restaurant scene that has "exploded" in the past five years.

According to Denver's tourism website, the neighborhood boasts 300 stores, 75 cafes and restaurants, 50 spas and salons, and five hotels.

According to recent reports, "It's really the walkability that appeals to everyone," she says. "It's like a large village. To be able to live in the neighborhood, and walk out the door in the morning, grab a cup of coffee or go work out before going into the office, it's very much a live-work place.".

Raymond, who has long represented top tier properties in the area, says that there are only three other luxury condos in the neighborhood—and none of them offer the level of service and amenities that the Waldorf does.

Affluent state residents were ready to pounce: An impressive 75% of the complex's units, or all but seven, are already sold. This includes four of the seven penthouses, as well as the most expensive penthouse, priced at $13 million.

Monthly HOA dues will be estimated about $1.50 per square foot, which will cover most amenities and services.

Raymond claims that the developer, PMG, "leaned on" the local brokerages, asking them what well-heeled buyers in the area wanted.

"We had a whole list of things people were looking for," she indicates. Top of the list for amenities was a fitness center—and the complex will have a wellness center with massage, sauna and steam rooms, as well as the now-requisite cold plunge.

According to recent reports, "A lot of people were asking about that," she notes with a laugh. "It's like taking two shots of espresso.".

There's also a resort rooftop pool, signature restaurant (still being negotiated), owners' lounge, and the Waldorf's signature Peacock Alley-inspired lounge and bar.

These affluent buyers are also busy—and crave as frictionless a lifestyle as possible.

"They value time, convenience, personalized service," she says. "That's really a hallmark of the Waldorf Astoria name.".

To that end, the concierge services will include valet, housekeeping, pet services, laundry, parcel reception, doorman and bellman, security, automotive detailing, chef services, and more.

In a recent development, personal concierge services are "a la carte," and could include requests such as finding a hotel for visiting family members, or procuring tickets to a hot theatrical production. An initial concierge meeting with a buyer will help pinpoint services that might be needed, says the broker.

Ownership also comes with discounts at both Waldorf Astoria and parent organization Hilton hotels worldwide.

Recent findings suggest that "What surprised me is how many local people were buying," indicates the agent. "I was thinking we'd be getting people from all over the country—which we did—but the initial run was all local people.".

She attributes the intense local interest to elite Colorado residents—who already own a ski chalet, mountain estate, or sprawling ranch—also wanting a "city place," as their second or even third abode.

But until a complex came along with a bold name like Waldorf Astoria, they couldn't find a place that met their high standards.

In a recent development, "A lot of the buyers had looked at the other condo buildings," she claims, but found them lacking. "They were waiting for something truly spectacular to come along.".

The Waldorf Astoria was "literally the perfect brand to come in," she says. "It's just brought so much excitement.".

Beyond generally being locals, the condo's buyers are a "diverse group," from CEOs to techies to "oil and gas people" to ranchers. "It's quite a mix of people," she says.

Since most of the buyers will be using the pads as pieds-à-terre, they wanted to know that everything will be taken care of for them awhile they were away, says the broker.

"They trust the name and brand. It's very special.".

Industry News: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning.
  • Researchers found that adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee developed dementia at considerably lower rates than those who rarely or never drank it.
  • The strongest associations appeared among people who drank two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning. A long-running study of U.S. adults suggests that drinking caffeinated coffee regularly is associated with a substantially lower risk of dementia and better cognitive health as people age.

Researchers found that adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee developed dementia at considerably lower rates than those who rarely or never drank it. The findings were based on follow-up periods extending as long as 43 years, offering a valuable look at how everyday drinking habits relate to brain health over time.

The strongest associations appeared among people who drank two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day. Tea consumption was also linked to better cognitive outcomes, although the amount associated with the greatest benefit was somewhat lower.

Interestingly, decaffeinated coffee did not show the same benefits, raising questions about whether caffeine itself might help explain the connection.

Coffee Drinkers Indicated Much Lower Dementia Rates.

One of the most striking findings involved the difference in dementia rates between regular coffee drinkers and people who consumed little or no coffee.

Among U.S. adults who drank higher amounts of caffeinated coffee, researchers recorded 141 dementia cases annually for every 100,000 people. In comparison, the rate was 330 cases per 100,000 people each year among those who rarely or never drank caffeinated coffee.

Sources indicate that dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with memory, thinking, reasoning, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer's disease is its most common cause, although several other brain disorders can also lead to dementia.

While occasional forgetfulness can be a normal part of aging, dementia involves cognitive difficulties severe enough to disrupt daily life. Identifying lifestyle habits associated with lower dementia risk is therefore an notable area of research, particularly as populations grow older.

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that regular caffeinated coffee consumption may be one such habit. However, the results show an association rather than proving that coffee directly prevents dementia. Other differences between coffee drinkers and people who avoid coffee could also contribute to the observed results.

Coffee Was Also Linked to Better Cognitive Health.

In a recent development, the potential benefits were not limited to diagnosed dementia. Participants who drank more caffeinated coffee were also less likely to report that their memory or thinking abilities had declined.

Researchers found that 7.8% of adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee reported subjective cognitive decline, compared with 9.5% of those who rarely or never drank it.

Subjective cognitive decline refers to changes in memory or thinking that people notice themselves, even when those difficulties have not necessarily been confirmed by formal cognitive testing. Someone experiencing it might feel that remembering information, concentrating, or finding the right words has become more difficult.

Such complaints do not automatically indicate dementia. Nevertheless, they can provide useful information about how people perceive changes in their cognitive abilities as they grow older.

The lower percentage among caffeinated coffee drinkers adds to the evidence linking coffee consumption with healthier cognitive aging.

How Much Coffee Offers the Greatest Benefit?

The researchers also examined whether the amount of coffee consumed was related to the strength of the observed benefits.

Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with the most favorable outcomes for dementia risk and cognitive functioning.

Notably, this association remained apparent regardless of participants' genetic risk of developing dementia. In other words, the relationship between coffee consumption and brain health was observed even among people whose inherited characteristics might make them more vulnerable to the disease.

Genetic risk refers to the influence of inherited variations in DNA that can increase or decrease a person's likelihood of developing certain conditions. Although genetics can play an crucial role in dementia, they are only one part of a much larger picture that includes age, general health, and lifestyle.

The results also suggest that drinking larger amounts of coffee is not necessarily better. Consumption beyond the range associated with the strongest benefits did not appear to provide additional protection.

Tea Drinkers May Benefit Too, but Decaf Was Different.

Recent findings suggest that coffee was not the only beverage associated with better brain health. Researchers found that drinking tea was also linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning.

According to recent reports, for tea, the strongest associations appeared among participants who consumed one to two cups per day. As with coffee, drinking more than this amount did not appear to produce further benefits.

However, the study did not distinguish between caffeinated and noncaffeinated tea. As a result, the findings cannot establish whether caffeine was responsible for the association observed among tea drinkers.

According to recent reports, the results for coffee offered an additional clue. While regular caffeinated coffee was associated with lower dementia risk and better cognitive outcomes, decaffeinated coffee did not demonstrate the same benefits.

Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee, tea, and several other plants. It acts on the central nervous system and is best known for temporarily increasing alertness and reducing feelings of tiredness.

Whether caffeine also contributes to better brain health over many years is a separate question. The difference between regular and decaffeinated coffee makes this possibility worth investigating, but it does not establish caffeine as the cause of the observed benefits.

Taken together, the findings suggest that moderate consumption of caffeinated coffee and tea may be associated with healthier brain aging. For coffee drinkers, two to three cups daily appeared to offer the strongest association, while one to two cups of tea indicated the most favorable results among tea drinkers.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these beverages directly influence dementia risk, the long-term findings offer encouraging news for people who already enjoy coffee or tea as part of their daily routine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Calibrate, Withings study finds wraparound care boosts GLP-1 weight loss by more than 60%" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—As health plans and employers continue to evaluate the costs and outcomes associated with GLP-1 weight loss drugs, a new study found that wraparound clinical care and behavior change support can make expensive GLP-1 treatments more effective and durable.

A two-year real-world study from Withings Health Solutions and Calibrate Health suggests that pairing GLP-1 medications with Calibrate’s integrated obesity care program produced substantially greater weight loss than GLP-1 treatment alone, and Calibrate members sustained more of their weight loss.

It has been revealed that the study followed 4,961 U.S. adults who began GLP-1s between 2022 and 2024, comparing 3,422 Calibrate members with 1,539 Withings consumers taking GLP-1s without the program. After adjustment for differences between the groups, Calibrate members lost 17.3% of their starting weight at two years versus 10.7% for the GLP-1-only group, a more than 60% relative difference.

The study was a real-world observational analysis, not a randomized controlled trial. Because Calibrate members chose to join the program, the two groups differed at the start. Before comparing, a statistical adjustment made them comparable on age, sex, race, BMI, health conditions and GLP-1 treatment. Weight was followed over 24 months.

The study findings, shared first with Fierce Healthcare, underscore that GLP-1 treatment may work better when medication is paired with personalized clinical management, behavioral coaching and continuous monitoring, rather than being treated primarily as a prescription benefit, according to Calibrate, a digitally integrated obesity management solution.

The study results also reinforce that obesity should be treated as a disease, another chronic metabolic condition requiring intensive, ongoing support, rather than a medication-only problem, Linda Anegawa, M.D., Calibrate Health’s chief medical advisor, told Fierce Healthcare.

Industry observers note that “With any chronic disease, like hypertension for example, you won’t get as good outcomes if you just hand someone a medication and don’t support them across other pillars of health, like self-monitoring blood pressure, physical activity, and stress reduction. Type 2 diabetes is another good example; you can give high doses of insulin, but medication can’t do the job alone without nutrition education and support,” she said.

“[The study results] make it very clear that treatment [for obesity] shouldn’t stop at just drug coverage,” she added. “As we envision the future, I’d like to see obesity care looking very similar to diabetes care, with insurance covering the full range of necessary services from medication treatment to nutrition education and overall lifestyle support. Obesity is a complex, chronic disease deserving of the same coverage parity as any other.".

Treating obesity as such not only prevents health complications and improves quality of life, but it will also lower overall long-term health systems’ costs of care, Anegawa asserted.

According to recent reports, the advantage of the integrated care program persisted despite weight regain, the study found. While both study groups regained some weight after reaching their lowest point, the Calibrate members remained about 16.6% below their starting weight, according to the study results. The GLP-1-only group reached a best point of 12.6% weight loss and was about 9.2% below baseline at the peak of its rebound.

There was a body-composition benefit as well. In a subgroup of 974 participants followed for body composition, the muscle-to-fat ratio improved 49.3% for Calibrate members versus 39.9% for GLP-1-only consumers at 18 months, roughly a 9-point difference.

In a recent development, the study data is based on two years of daily weigh-ins from Withings connected scales, analyzed with causal-inference methods. Body composition was followed over 18 months in 520 Calibrate members and 454 Withings people.

The study reinforces the importance of evaluating body composition, rather than weight alone, in obesity treatment, Anegawa said.

“We know that abnormal visceral fat accumulation and dysfunction is what drives most of the metabolic conditions we treat, so if we aren’t equipping members to maximize visceral fat loss and preserve muscle, we can actually end up making people sicker. Losing muscle has severe consequences—it isn’t just scaffolding. Muscle is a critical metabolic organ that regulates energy balance, hormonal signaling, and insulin sensitivity,” she said.

Adding the insights of body composition to Calibrate's clinical and metabolic data allows the firm to better monitor trends and adapt care based on quality evidence, she noted.

There are several key factors that make an integrated obesity care program more effective than a medication-only program, Anegawa said.

"Physician-led personalized care that includes medication optimization for each member’s needs, tailored wraparound support, and features that drive continuous engagement—all of which are designed to maximize clinical outcomes," she stated.

"Breaking this down, we start with a comprehensive clinical evaluation for each member, vs. other programs which only require a questionnaire for a prescription. This helps us get to know each member’s medical and weight histories in detail. We analyze comprehensive lab data to understand their baseline metabolic profile. This information is then used by our expert clinicians to personalize clinical care from day one," Anegawa noted.

Live one-to-one coaching support focuses on four pillars of healthy weight maintenance: nutrition, activity, sleep and mindset shift. Tailored education and anticipatory guidance help members manage side effects and stay on treatment, while connecting members to their personal motivations helps sustain engagement through challenges and supports lasting improvements in metabolic health, according to Calibrate.

Calibrate Health has been working with connected health device maker Withings for over five years. The tech giant's members use Withings devices regularly as a required part of the program, according to Anegawa.

According to recent reports, "We were already getting body composition data that gave us additional insights into individual members’ health. That data led to additional questions, such as are there significant differences that we can see in aggregate? If so, how large are the differences, and are they changing clinical outcomes? Can we use these data to inform and improve the evolution of our protocols and clinical care? So in asking these types of questions, it became clear to both the Calibrate and Withings teams that we should formalize this into a collaborative study," she noted.

The use of smart devices, specifically Wi-Fi or Bluetooth-connected scales, provides continuous data to help identify weight loss patterns that might not have been apparent through traditional clinical measures, noted Antoine Pivron, vice president of Withings Health Solutions.

Sources indicate that "Today, most people on a GLP-1 are monitored through a keyhole. A patient whose primary care doctor prescribes the drug might be weighed a few times a year, and each reading reflects one day: what they ate, the time, the clothes they wore. Between visits, nobody knows whether they plateaued in month three, started regaining in month five, or stopped the drug altogether," he said.

According to recent reports, "Specialty programs do better, but many rely on self-reported weights from whatever scale the patient owns. And people tend to stop reporting exactly when things go wrong, which is the moment the care team most needs to know," he added.

It has been revealed that body composition is the biggest blind spot, Pivron asserted. Withings' smart scales track weight and detailed body composition metrics to help identify whether the weight coming off during treatment is fat or muscle.

Recent findings suggest that "In the study we did with Calibrate, two years of data let us see the full shape of the journey: the drop, the low point, and the partial regain that follows. We could also see the quality of the weight loss, not just the quantity. Program members improved their muscle-to-fat balance more, but part of their extra weight loss was muscle. That tells a program exactly where to focus next: protein and strength training," Pivron noted.

Withings, a French consumer electronics tech giant, rolled out its B2B health solutions division in 2019 to meet the growing market around virtual care and remote management in the U.S.

Pivron expects connected health devices like smart scales to play a growing role in GLP-1 treatment programs and broader chronic disease management.

Recent findings suggest that "A GLP-1 prescription isn’t a care plan. The programs that work combine three things: the drug, the clinical and coaching support around it, and the data that shows whether it’s working. Miss one, and real-world results rarely match what we see in trials," he remarked.

Body composition will become standard in GLP-1 care, Pivron asserted: "That’s where the clinical definition of obesity is already heading.".

Connected devices provide the data layer—continuously tracking weight and body composition, predicting when patients may be veering off course and identifying additional risks such as hypertension.

"But a risk score is not a diagnosis. A notification with no next step just creates anxiety. These signals belong inside a care program with a protocol: confirm with a cuff, see a clinician, treat if needed," he said. "Employers and payers are moving toward paying for outcomes. Connected devices are how a program proves it delivered them.".

Employers face rising healthcare costs—projected to climb 9.5% next year—and GLP-1 treatments are a major contributor to that cost growth.

The study provides evidence of better outcomes with wraparound care, but it did not evaluate the impact on healthcare spending.

Anegawa contends that improvements in markers associated with high metabolic risk, like Hemoglobin A1c, the liver enzyme ALT and lipids, would point to meaningful cost savings.

Calibrate data from separate evaluations show substantial improvements in these markers among Calibrate members.

“Among Calibrate members who started the program with diabetes or prediabetes, 80% reached normoglycemic status at one year. Among those with abnormal ALT, 79% shifted to the normal range, and 68% of those with abnormal triglycerides were normal at year one," she said.

Withings' body composition data builds on Calibrate's prior data and gives the organization another lens on the whole picture, "suggesting that lower healthcare spend is likely,” Anegawa noted.

Greater treatment persistence could also ultimately reduce costs. An integrated approach helps keep members engaged so they stick with treatment and get the full benefit of therapy, she noted.

Along with weight loss and metabolic improvements, Calibrate members also report compelling health and productivity outcomes, Anegawa said. Among members with a high work-related burden at intake, 82% no longer reported it at one year.

“My favorite evidence of all is that 90% report that Calibrate improved their overall quality of life, and 94% say that their health is better than a year ago - the most clinically meaningful to me overall,” she said.

Modernist architect Jules Gregory’s iconic "Wave House," which was offered together with a sleek studio in Lambertville, NJ, earlier this year is now available for individual purchase.

In a recent development, “The condo status was recently approved, so now you can get the Wave House for $1.65 million, the studio for $995,000, or both for $2.6 million,” says listing agent Grant Wagner of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty. “What makes this unique is if you wanted to buy both, you have the option to sell one later.”.

Built in 1960, the four-bedroom primary residence, known for its wavy roofline, has 1,700 square feet of midcentury space, including curvy wood ceilings that rise and dip above the rooms, glass walls and doors, exposed beams, stone details, and oversized windows framing the picturesque lot.

“The Wave House will attract an architecture enthusiast drawn to its dramatic roofline, spaces that expand and compress, expanses of glass, and privacy,” Wagner says. “Being such a rare offering, it could easily bring a buyer from New York, Philadelphia, or abroad—someone who wants to own a piece of art in an architectural sense.”.

With ceilings that appear to float above the living areas, the open floor strategy also has a sunken conversation lounge, a beamed living room, and a European-inspired kitchen.

The detached studio has a 1,200-square-foot open floor proposal with two en suite bedrooms and upcoming baths. The chef’s kitchen has a waterfall island, a “jewel box-inspired” accent wall, and “cleverly concealed” storage and a fridge/freezer behind matching doors.

A beamed living room has a decorative fireplace. Double atrium doors open to a bluestone patio overlooking a vegetable garden and the beautifully landscaped lot. Other highlights include newly introduced lighting, windows, HVAC, and “countless other upgrades.”.

It has been revealed that “The studio will likely speak to someone seeking a sophisticated, sexy weekend pied-à-terre, an architecture lover who prefers a more minimalist aesthetic and turnkey, come-and-go lifestyle,” Wagner notes. “You can walk out, and it lives like a condo.”.

Located on a combined 10.03 acres (the Wave House sits on approximately 6 acres and the studio offers 4 acres of privacy), the homes are also near the 70-mile Delaware & Raritan Canal State Park Trail for hiking and biking.

“They are very unique offerings,” he adds. “While it would be cool to own both, you can also buy a piece of art while looking at one, too.”.
