#6336. Industry News: Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1504 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major clinical trial has raised new questions about how doctors decide who should take statins to prevent heart attacks and strokes.
  • The findings, presented during a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026, also revealed a striking difference in how consistently patients took their medication.
  • Recent findings suggest that although the results suggest that heart scans could help doctors make more targeted treatment decisions, the trial did not establish that the scan approach was as effective as conventional risk assessment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major clinical trial has raised new questions about how doctors decide who should take statins to prevent heart attacks and strokes. Researchers found that using heart scans to guide treatment decisions produced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, even though the scans led to far fewer recommendations to begin taking statins.

The findings, presented during a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026, also revealed a striking difference in how consistently patients took their medication. Those advised to use statins based on calcium buildup in their coronary arteries were substantially more likely to follow their treatment recommendations.

Recent findings suggest that although the results suggest that heart scans could help doctors make more targeted treatment decisions, the trial did not establish that the scan approach was as effective as conventional risk assessment. Researchers say additional studies are needed to determine whether it offers a better strategy for preventing cardiovascular disease.

Why Predicting Heart Disease Risk Remains a Challenge.

Cardiovascular disease remains the world's leading cause of illness and death. Much of this burden comes from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), which develops when fatty deposits known as plaque accumulate inside arteries, restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Coronary artery disease and ischemic stroke are two major forms of this condition.

Several common factors increase the likelihood of developing ASCVD, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, and elevated cholesterol. Doctors use these factors to estimate a person's cardiovascular risk and determine whether preventive medications are appropriate.

In a recent development, statins are among the most widely used treatments for lowering that risk. These medications reduce cholesterol levels, particularly low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called LDL or bad cholesterol. They also help lower the likelihood of serious cardiovascular complications.

According to recent reports, however, identifying which patients stand to benefit from statins remains a significant challenge. Some people who eventually experience a heart attack do not appear to be at particularly high risk under conventional screening methods.

"For far too many patients, the first symptom of ASCVD is a heart attack," said Doctor Joseph B Muhlestein from the Intermountain Medical Center, Murray, USA, the Principal Investigator of the CorCal Outcomes trial. "Statins have been shown to be highly effective in the prevention of ASCVD; however, there is a major gap in risk assessment, statin initiation, and statin persistence.".

According to Muhlestein, many people who suffer their first heart attack, particularly younger adults, would not previously have been classified as having enough cardiovascular risk to justify statin treatment. This limitation has prompted researchers to investigate whether directly examining the arteries might provide more useful information.

Can Heart Calcium Scans Improve Statin Decisions?

The CorCal Outcomes trial investigated two different approaches for determining which patients should be advised to begin statin therapy before experiencing a cardiovascular event.

The first relied on the pooled cohort equations (PCE), a commonly used risk assessment tool that estimates cardiovascular risk using traditional factors such as age, cholesterol levels, blood pressure, and smoking status.

The second approach measured coronary artery calcium (CAC), which provides a more direct indication of plaque buildup in the arteries supplying the heart.

According to recent reports, this measurement uses a computed tomography (CT) scan to detect calcium deposits in the coronary arteries. Calcium can accumulate within atherosclerotic plaque, making it a useful marker of underlying coronary artery disease, even in people who have not developed symptoms.

Unlike traditional risk calculators, which estimate the likelihood of future cardiovascular problems based on personal characteristics and health measurements, calcium scans provide evidence of disease already present in the coronary arteries.

Researchers wanted to determine whether using this information to guide statin recommendations could improve cardiovascular outcomes.

Nearly 5,800 Patients Put Both Methods to the Test.

The trial enrolled 5,772 patients from the Canyons and Desert regions of Intermountain Health Care in the United States. Participants had no known history of ASCVD or diabetes and had not previously received statin therapy.

Their average age was 64, and women accounted for 51% of the study population.

Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to one of two groups. One group received statin treatment guidance based on traditional cardiovascular risk scores, while the other received recommendations based on coronary calcium scan results.

Both patients and their physicians were informed of the treatment recommendations generated by the study protocol. However, the final decision about whether to start taking statins remained with the patients and their doctors.

The researchers then tracked major cardiovascular events (MACE; all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and arterial revascularization).

This combined outcome included death from any cause, heart attacks, strokes, and procedures to restore blood flow through narrowed or blocked arteries.

Heart Scans Led to Far Fewer Statin Recommendations.

After an average follow-up of 4.2 years, researchers found that major cardiovascular events occurred at exactly the same observed rate in both groups.

It has been revealed that A total of 2.7% of patients in each group experienced one of the events included in the study's primary outcome. The estimated relative risk over time was also nearly identical (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% confidence interval 0.71 to 1.38; p=0.045 for noninferiority).

In a recent development, however, this similarity did not establish that the two strategies were equally effective. The study failed to meet its predetermined statistical requirement for demonstrating that the calcium scan approach was not meaningfully worse than conventional risk assessment.

A notable difference emerged in how frequently patients were advised to begin taking statins.

Participants evaluated using traditional risk scores received recommendations to start statin therapy more than three times as often as those whose decisions were guided by coronary calcium measurements.

Despite this substantial difference in treatment recommendations, both groups experienced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events during the follow-up period.

A Surprising Difference in Statin Adherence.

Perhaps the most intriguing finding involved whether patients actually followed their prescribed treatment.

Among those advised to take statins, patients whose recommendations were based on calcium scans were much more likely to adhere to their medication regimen than those assessed using traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

It has been revealed that the difference was substantial (62% vs. 23%).

In other words, patients recommended statins based on visible evidence of calcium buildup in their arteries were approximately 2.7 times as likely to follow their medication regimen.

Recent findings suggest that one possible explanation is that seeing evidence of disease in their own arteries makes patients more motivated to take preventive medication. However, the trial did not establish why adherence differed so dramatically between the groups.

The findings raise the possibility that coronary calcium scans could influence not only which patients receive statin recommendations, but also whether those patients consistently take the medications.

What the Findings Mean for Heart Disease Prevention.

Despite these potentially key differences, the researchers emphasized that the study could not establish whether calcium scan-guided treatment provides cardiovascular protection comparable to traditional risk assessment.

One notable limitation was that fewer participants experienced major cardiovascular events than the investigators had anticipated. With fewer events to analyze, the trial had less statistical power to determine whether a meaningful difference existed between the two approaches.

It has been revealed that "The power of the study to detect a difference was reduced by the lower-than-expected event rates and we did not demonstrate noninferiority between the groups," mentioned Doctor Muhlestein, who concluded: "The study did provide vital hypothesis-generating insights into the efficiency of statin initiation and adherence when decisions are based on CAC scoring. Taken together, our data could be used to plan an additional well-powered randomized trial comparing CAC with current risk factor-based algorithms.".

The findings may help researchers design future trials capable of determining whether coronary calcium scans can improve the efficiency of statin prescribing without compromising cardiovascular protection.

Recent findings suggest that current European recommendations already recognize a potential role for these measurements. The 2025 Focused Update of the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidemias recommends considering increased coronary calcium scores, when available, as an additional factor in cardiovascular risk assessment.

This guidance applies particularly to people at moderate cardiovascular risk or those whose estimated risk falls near the threshold at which preventive medication would normally be recommended.

For these individuals, evidence of calcium buildup may help doctors make more informed decisions when the need for statin therapy is uncertain.

Recent findings suggest that the CorCal Outcomes findings add to the discussion by suggesting that heart scans may also influence how faithfully patients follow treatment. Whether that advantage translates into better long-term cardiovascular outcomes remains an vital question for future research.

HLTH 2026: Viz.ai, Wolters Kluwer partner on platform integration" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Artificial intelligence-driven disease detection and intelligent care platform Viz.ai revealed Monday a strategic partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI.

Through the partnership, providers caring for patients with complex conditions will be able to ask detailed questions and receive evidence-based answers relevant to clinical context from UpToDate directly within existing workflows.

“The greatest leap we can achieve in healthcare is to make the best medical evidence always available, applied automatically to every patient, at the moment it matters,” mentioned Chris Mansi, Viz.ai CEO and co-founder, in a statement to Fierce Healthcare.

Mansi continued, “Bringing UpToDate’s trusted evidence into Viz.ai’s workflow takes us closer to that vision: an AI safety net that detects disease, helps clinicians identify who needs care and empower them to act on the evidence. Our goal is to close the gap between what medicine knows and the care each patient receives, so no patient is left behind.”.

The companies say it is the first integration to bring UpToDate into AI-driven care coordination workflows.

Wolters Kluwer CEO Greg Samios stated in a statement that one of healthcare AI’s biggest opportunities is "to help clinicians see more of the patient's full picture when making healthcare decisions.".

“Viz.ai's technology can proactively flag signs of disease and alert care teams, even before a condition is suspected,” Samios said. “Paired with UpToDate's trusted clinical intelligence, clinicians have more of the information they need, directly in their workflow, to help inform care decisions.”.

#6332. Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1051 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A fresh national study suggests that the way people consume cannabis may reveal vital clues about their likelihood of using it heavily or developing an addiction.
  • Cannabis is consumed in several ways, including smoking, vaping, eating edibles, and dabbing, which involves heating concentrated cannabis products and inhaling the resulting vapor.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at NYU Langone Health identified four distinct patterns of cannabis consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A fresh national study suggests that the way people consume cannabis may reveal vital clues about their likelihood of using it heavily or developing an addiction. While smoking remains the most popular method among US adults who use cannabis, roughly one in seven consumes it in nearly every available form. Researchers found that this group had particularly high rates of daily use and cannabis use disorder.

Cannabis is consumed in several ways, including smoking, vaping, eating edibles, and dabbing, which involves heating concentrated cannabis products and inhaling the resulting vapor. Its use is widespread in the United States. Recent national survey figures indicate that approximately 43.8 million Americans ages 12 and older (more than 15 percent) had consumed cannabis within the previous 30 days.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at NYU Langone Health identified four distinct patterns of cannabis consumption. Nearly half of users, 48 percent, primarily smoked cannabis, while 21 percent combined smoking and vaping. Another 17 percent mainly consumed edibles. The remaining 14 percent belonged to what researchers called the "polymodal group," meaning they used cannabis in almost every available form.

Cannabis Addiction Rates Differ Sharply by Consumption Pattern.

Recent findings suggest that the findings, published online August 8 in the journal Addictive Behaviors, revealed major differences in how frequently these groups consumed cannabis. Approximately half of people in the polymodal group reported using it every day. Daily use was considerably less common among other participants, occurring in 28 percent of those who primarily smoked, 31 percent of those who smoked and vaped, and about 13 percent of those who mainly consumed edibles.

In a recent development, an even more striking difference emerged when researchers examined cannabis use disorder, the medical diagnosis associated with cannabis addiction. About 67 percent of polymodal users met the criteria for the disorder, compared with 47 percent of those who both smoked and vaped, 36 percent of those who mainly smoked, and just 15 percent of participants who primarily used edibles.

It has been revealed that "Our findings suggest that using cannabis in multiple forms may be a red flag for heavier use and symptoms of addiction," mentioned study lead author Omar El-Shahawy, MD, PhD, MPH, an assistant professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. "Asking patients not only whether but how they use cannabis could help clinicians identify when a fuller assessment may be warranted.".

To investigate these patterns, the research team examined responses from 17,732 adults who had used cannabis during the preceding month. The information came from the 2022-2023 National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Using statistical methods to identify similarities in participants' consumption habits, the researchers conducted the first national analysis of how different methods of cannabis use naturally group together.

Younger Adults More Likely to Use Multiple Forms of Cannabis.

The researchers also discovered notable differences in the characteristics of people who preferred particular consumption methods. Young adults ages 18 to 25 accounted for nearly one-third of both the smoking and vaping group and the polymodal group. In contrast, only about one sixth of participants who primarily smoked cannabis belonged to that age range.

Edibles showed a different demographic pattern. Women made up more than half of those who mainly consumed edible cannabis products, and this method was particularly common among college graduates. However, the study did not investigate what motivated participants to choose specific consumption methods, leaving the reasons for these differences unresolved, according to Dr. El-Shahawy.

According to recent reports, another finding raised concerns about the potential effects of inhaling smoke. People who smoked cannabis were more likely to also smoke cigarettes than those who mainly vaped cannabis or consumed edibles. Because both tobacco and cannabis smoking involve combustion (burning), people who regularly smoke both substances may expose their lungs to additional harmful chemicals.

Industry observers note that "The strong tie between smoking cannabis and smoking cigarettes is of concern because this subset of people are breathing in a wider range of chemicals via combustion, and their lungs are at risk," said senior author Joseph J. Palamar, PhD, MPH, a professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

Why Cannabis Prevention Messages May Need to Change.

Sources indicate that the findings suggest that health education should account for the different ways people consume cannabis rather than concentrating primarily on smoking. Different consumption patterns may call for different approaches to explaining potential risks, particularly among younger adults and people who regularly combine several methods.

It has been revealed that "Public health messages about cannabis still focus mostly on smoking, but people now use the drug in many different ways," stated Dr. El-Shahawy. "For younger adults, that means talking about the risks of vaping and combining multiple forms, while for people who prefer edibles, the message is to 'start low and go slow' because the effects take time to kick in.".

The researchers hope to investigate the motivations behind these consumption patterns in future work. According to Dr. El-Shahawy, one question is whether people who favor edibles are more likely to use cannabis to manage problems such as pain or difficulty sleeping.

According to recent reports, the team also emphasized several limitations. Because participants described their own cannabis habits, some may not have reported their consumption accurately or completely. The observational study also cannot determine whether using multiple forms of cannabis directly increases addiction risk. It establishes an association between consumption patterns and cannabis use disorder, rather than proving that one causes the other.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health through grant R01DA055675.

In a recent development, additional NYU Langone researchers who contributed to the study included Mohsen Abbasi-Kangevari, MD, MPH; Michelle He; and Xiaoying Zheng, alongside Drs. El-Shahawy and Palamar. Neal Doran, PhD, of the University of California, San Diego, also served as a study co-investigator.

Materials provided by NYU Langone Health / NYU Grossman School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Measles update: US loses measles elimination status; more deaths reported" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, and has now exceeded 5,400 cases and 10 total measles-associated deaths in 2026.

The status determination from the Pan American Health Organization, which is part of the World Health Organization, was made late last week and first reported by the Wall Street Journal before being confirmed by other outlets. The public health body had planned to make the announcement public on Tuesday.

It has been revealed that the U.S. had notched elimination status, reflecting no continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months, in 2000. Regaining it similarly requires the country to stop continuous spread for 12 months. PAHO recommends countries that have lost elimination status submit and enact a corrective action strategy that includes immunization and surveillance.

The decision landed shortly after the country hit 5,412 confirmed measles cases, per a Nov. 13 enhancement from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

Industry observers note that health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, mentioned in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is notable for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.".

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a upcoming standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

The Latest York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

Industry observers note that the state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Recent findings suggest that sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department stated. Many of Upcoming York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

Recent findings suggest that in a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease.".

"This is Newly introduced York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

It has been revealed that as of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone stated they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

In a recent development, A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to Fresh York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they mentioned.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to Upcoming York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they stated.

Industry observers note that "Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

Sources indicate that the vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and upcoming CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not introduced the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

In a recent development, pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry.
  • The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers.
  • The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in Newly introduced York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

According to recent reports, audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

It has been revealed that the broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:.

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

Hell, some men do it even if they’re not experiencing hair loss—and that’s cool, too. Investing in a quality head shaver will double down on the convenience factor of being bald by making the entire process seamless.

When you do choose to shave your head, the tools you use to do it are paramount. That’s where the best head shavers come in. These high-tech gadgets are specifically designed to make shaving your head easier, whether it’s through a multi-head ergonomic design or close-cutting technology (or both).

Industry observers note that far easier than heading to the barbershop every few days, these electric shavers are meant to be used at home. Think of them as an easier, safer, and quicker alternative to carefully taking a razor to your dome. Most head shavers on this list can be used dry, which means as long as your hair is already short enough (no more than a couple of days of growth), you can shave with no moisture or product. What's also great is that some options are waterproof, making your shaving experience in the shower a total breeze and easy to clean up.

Plus, you can use most wet/dry shavers with shaving products, so if you prefer to begin with a pre-shave oil to protect your scalp and then add a shaving cream or lotion to help with gliding. However, there are a couple of options we recommend that do not have this capability, so if you’re a dedicated shower shaver, focus solely on the wet/dry devices.

Industry observers note that A good cordless head shaver can last as long as 90 minutes, which means you can go a whole week without charging the battery. They also unlock the ability to shave in the shower or on the road without having to be plugged in. If you're constantly on the move and shave your head regularly, you will find that cordless options offer lots of convenience and save even more time.

In a recent development, even before joining the bald brotherhood, most of us have all had an electric razor or beard trimmer die out before we've finished the job. Nobody wants to sport a half-trimmed beard or uneven body hair, but the absolute last spot you'll want an uneven shave is on your dome, as it's the hardest to hide.

Sources indicate that to avoid walking around with a patchy skull, keep battery life in mind when choosing an electric shaver. Consider how long you typically take to shave your entire head—and how often you tend to charge devices—before finalizing your decision.

Recent findings suggest that the first question to ask is: Does this shaver come with a case included? If yes, then you're going to want to look at what type of case it is. After much anticipation, internationally acclaimed architect Robert Oshatz has unveiled his latest architectural tour de force, a jaw-dropping, ultra-modern residence in Portland’s West Hills neighborhood.

In a recent development, listed for $2,888,000, the newly completed home was designed by Oshatz, an apprentice of Frank Lloyd Wright Jr. It is one of five planned homes tucked into the forest, four of which have yet to be built.

Recent findings suggest that “It took about three years, but it is finally complete,” stated listing agent Terry Sprague of LUXE | Forbes Global Properties. “Robert Oshatz is like the Andy Warhol/Peter Max of real estate. His designs are so completely unusual compared to commoditized architecture.”.

The four-bedroom home’s steel-framed structure has curved wood ceilings, circular windows, disappearing glass walls, and an elevator that provides easy access to all four levels.

Sprague believes the residence will likely be used as a second or third home.

A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have identified a protein that may play an notable role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin.
  • In a recent development, the protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes.
  • The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have identified a protein that may play an notable role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin. The discovery could provide a promising latest target for treatments designed to improve blood sugar control.

In a recent development, the protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes. In preclinical experiments, scientists discovered that removing Miro1 restored the muscles' response to insulin. They also found that exercise lowered Miro1 levels in people with the disease, offering new insight into how physical activity improves insulin sensitivity.

The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.

How a Hidden Muscle Protein Affects Insulin Resistance.

Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) is located on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells responsible for producing energy. Researchers believe that excessive amounts of this protein may interfere with how muscles respond to insulin, making it more difficult for the body to regulate blood sugar effectively.

It has been revealed that to investigate this connection, the research team studied Miro1 in laboratory cells, preclinical models, and people living with Type 2 diabetes. By examining the protein across these different settings, they were able to explore its effects on muscle function and determine whether the findings could be relevant to human disease.

The results revealed that Miro1 buildup impaired the muscles' response to insulin. When researchers removed the protein in preclinical models, insulin responsiveness returned, providing evidence that Miro1 contributes directly to this process.

Exercise Reduces a Protein Linked to Type 2 Diabetes.

It has been revealed that the researchers also investigated whether exercise could influence Miro1 levels in people with diabetes. In a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care.

People assigned to the exercise group experienced a decline in Miro1 levels in their muscles. These changes occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles' capacity to produce energy.

The findings suggest that reducing Miro1 may be one of the ways exercise helps the body respond more effectively to insulin. They also raise the possibility that treatments designed to target the protein could eventually provide additional benefits alongside physical activity.

"Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle's response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it," said Dr. John P. Kirwan, the study's senior author.

A Promising Newly introduced Direction for Diabetes Treatment.

Industry observers note that kirwan recently became executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma. He carried out the research while working at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and has since brought his internationally recognized translational research program to the University of Oklahoma.

He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the university and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

Industry observers note that the study's first author, Elizabeth Heintz, is a doctoral candidate who worked in the Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory at Pennington Biomedical. Christopher Axelrod, the study's co-corresponding author, has also moved to the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, joining Kirwan in continuing this line of research.

It has been revealed that dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical, emphasized the importance of connecting laboratory discoveries with research involving patients and broader populations.

"This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health," stated Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. "Dr. Kirwan and his team's findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment.".

Could Targeting Miro1 Lead to Fresh Diabetes Therapies?

Although the results are encouraging, scientists still need to establish whether directly targeting Miro1 can produce safe and effective treatments for people with Type 2 diabetes. The restoration of insulin responsiveness was demonstrated in preclinical models, while the human trial showed that exercise reduced Miro1 levels alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity.

Kirwan intends to continue investigating these findings at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. His research will combine laboratory experiments with studies involving people to uncover more of the biological mechanisms responsible for diabetes and explore fresh strategies for preventing and treating the condition.

Sources indicate that "Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally," he remarked. "Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution.".

The study received funding from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

HLTH 2026: CVS Health, Cigna and Abridge collaborating with OpenAI to test computer-use agents" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—OpenAI is expanding computer-use agents for healthcare, enabling AI to navigate electronic health record systems, payer portals and other software to tackle repetitive and manual tasks.

Computer-use agents, also called computer-using agents, are AI systems designed to interact with software interfaces the same way a human does—by viewing a screen, moving a cursor, clicking buttons and typing text.

Research teams at OpenAI have been exploring how computer-use agents can assist healthcare teams with fragmented clinical and administrative workflows while keeping people in control, Karan Singhal, head of Health AI and Artificial General Intelligence at OpenAI, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Around six months ago we set a research bet that we thought that the abilities for agents to use computers would end up being helpful and reliable enough in healthcare to help people with clinical and administrative workflows," Singhal said in an exclusive interview sharing evaluation results on OpenAI's early work with computer-use agents in healthcare.

Singhal also shed light on how OpenAI is working with CVS Health, Cigna Healthcare, Abridge and Ambience to apply computer-use agents to specific workflows, including referrals, prior authorizations, discharge planning, specialist consults and care manager preparation.

According to recent reports, healthcare systems are often disconnected, forcing administrative staff and care teams to manually move information from one system to another before a patient can get care. If a clinician orders an MRI, for example, the insurer may need information from the patient’s medical record, but a staff member still has to pull that information and enter it into a separate portal to request authorization.

OpenAI executives and researchers framed computer use as the next step in healthcare AI, moving beyond copilots that draft or summarize information to agents that can actually navigate EHRs, payer portals and other applications on a user's behalf.

Computer-use agents can bridge healthcare's fragmented software environment, especially where application programming interfaces (APIs) and other integrations don't exist or don't connect an entire workflow, Singhal noted.

Industry observers note that "We have been working with health systems on things like ChatGPT for Healthcare and our integration with Epic, but there are still limitations in how useful AI agents can be today. Computer use is really a way of resolving a lot of these barriers that exist between AI capabilities and healthcare software so that care teams can deliver better care, more effectively and more efficiently," he stated.

OpenAI continues to invest in APIs, plugins and MCP connectors to integrate AI with healthcare software, but the industry’s fragmented and legacy technology can make those integrations slow and incomplete, Singhal remarked. Computer use can help bridge those gaps by allowing AI to work across existing software interfaces and take on manual, repetitive workflows.

"What we hope to do with this release is move us closer to a world where, because AI is connected to more services, AI can help more with a lot of these workflows," he noted.

Care teams, developers and individual clinicians can access computer use for healthcare through ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians and the OpenAI API.

In a research demonstration using synthetic patient data, OpenAI highlighted how a computer-use agent could support a clinician and an authorization specialist working on the same MRI request. In the demonstration video, a patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. The clinician then instructs the computer-use agent to review the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records and prior imaging in the EHR. The computer-use agent drafts an MRI order, an encounter note and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review.

In the same demo video, the agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.

"The clinician and authorization specialist were both completely in control of their workflow, but the computer-use agent was able to help across different parts of the workflow and translate that into action," Singhal noted about the demo video.

OpenAI evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders, and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task, according to an OpenAI blog post.

Sources indicate that openAI says its GPT-6 Astra model can perform multi-step EHR tasks such as reviewing patient records, drafting messages and notes, preparing medication refills and proposing orders, while leaving key actions for clinician review. In OpenAI's evaluation, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated clinically safe, while physicians rated the model "very helpful" or "extremely helpful" in 93% of 646 assessments.

Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm, OpenAI stated.

Recent findings suggest that regarding the 1% of tasks rated not clinically safe, Singal said researchers did not identify any cases where the model created a specific, plausible risk of patient harm. "In some cases, the model might overreach and might take an action without getting the proper sign-off or authorization," he said.

"The models are not perfect today, and what we're sharing is an update on research results where we're seeing this critical point where the models seem to be useful in practice," he added.

OpenAI researchers also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals and medical equipment orders.

According to recent reports, openAI designed its computer-use agents with robust safeguards and data security in place, according to the manufacturer. The agents can be configured with limits on system access and actions, and audit logs provide a clear record of agent actions and approvals, giving healthcare teams visibility into how each workflow was completed.

Organizations are developing, piloting and deploying computer-use applications across a range of workflows and administrative tasks.

Sources indicate that CVS Health is using OpenAI’s computer-use capabilities to automate repetitive work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals and supporting specialist consults. In one production workflow, an agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend, OpenAI detailed in the blog post. Another agent handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day.

It has been revealed that generative AI organization Abridge is building computer-use agents to help clinicians carry out care plans across use cases and applications they use daily, including those without APIs. The company also plans to develop an inpatient use case, adding EHR information and nurse and clinician context to identify what needs attention and to coordinate next steps. As an example, agents can work concurrently on medication access and home health coordination, using computer interaction alongside calls and messages.

Recent findings suggest that cigna Healthcare is using OpenAI’s models to pull together member information from more than 10 clinical and administrative systems, including benefits, providers, appointments and previous interactions. The goal is to reduce the time case managers spend searching across systems and give them more time to support members, OpenAI wrote in the blog post.

Companies including Assort, Bunkerhill, Forus, Gravity and Tennr are testing agents that interact directly with EHRs and payer portals for referral management, authorization checks, medication approvals and other operational tasks.

It has been revealed that “We're continuing to invest in the models, making the models better at computer use. An important way that we think that they could continue to improve is around improved latency and costs,” Singhal noted.

In a recent development, openAI sees its role in healthcare as building foundational AI capabilities and letting healthcare companies handle the “last mile” of implementation, Singhal noted. Computer use is one example: OpenAI provides the technology and safeguards, while partners apply it to specialized workflows and deploy it within healthcare organizations.

The company also declared today improvements to trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates and cites medical evidence. OpenAI also expanded its healthcare plugin ecosystem with more than 20 latest healthcare plugins from companies across clinical care, care coordination and business operations.

#6321. Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1409 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that protein is everywhere these days.
  • After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan.
  • The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

In a recent development, "It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," states Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences.".

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity.

In a recent development, scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

It has been revealed that experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

According to recent reports, human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an key indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need.

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly key with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

In a recent development, research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching latest highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Sources indicate that their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging.

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

These effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

Industry observers note that studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

Researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging.

The amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an notable role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially key: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

Research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

According to recent reports, limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming states.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein.

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

It has been revealed that pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

Sources indicate that this distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming says. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are.".

In a recent development, the findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

The Permanente Medical Group confirmed on Monday the launch of a physician-led innovation organization it remarked will strike technology partnerships to co-develop, incubate and launch new enterprise healthcare delivery technologies.

Permanentech—a wholly owned subsidiary of the 10,000-physician medical group, which is itself part of the massive integrated nonprofit Kaiser Permanente—looks to rapidly advance potential latest healthcare offerings informed by its frontline physicians and the broader organization’s focus on value-based care.

According to recent reports, it marked the launch by announcing its first portfolio company: Wrapt Health, which offers an automated tool that predicts likely missed medical appointments for early outreach and rescheduling. In line with Permanentech’s broader thesis, it was born from a TPMG physician’s experiences, validated within the medical group and so far scaled to 22 sites in Kaiser Permanente’s Northern California region.

Industry observers note that “Our clinicians are continuously innovating and refining how we deliver care,” Kenneth Trauner, M.D., CEO of Permanentech and chief innovation officer at TPMG, mentioned in a release. “Permanentech gives them a dedicated resource to rapidly turn their insights and creativity into scalable solutions that benefit both our patients and the wider health care community.”.

Permanentech will be focused on technologies and AI-enabled tools addressing patient service, access and quality, TPMG remarked, with successful products also having the potential to improve “the economics of care delivery.” The business is structured “to move at the pace of the technology industry,” but has “a clear advantage” via its access to TPMG and Kaiser Permanente’s substantial footprint for deployment and validation, it said.

Those efforts will involve both home-grown tools and those developed by established or early-stage partners.

The former will champion physician-developed tools created inside TPMG’s ecosystem as independent manufacturer launches. Starting from the concept phase, that support would include financing as well as clinical and operational validation, as was the case with Wrapt Health.

In a recent development, “Our physicians and care teams see every day where technology can make care better,” Kristine Lee, M.D., an associate executive director and chief transformation officer at TPMG, stated. “Permanentech gives them a real hand in building tools that lift administrative burden and give time back to patients. When clinicians help build the tools, those tools fit the way they actually work.”.

Strategic partnerships and joint ventures, meanwhile, will focus on co-development, clinical valuation and scaled deployment. Permanentech said the latter will begin with local deployments that are expanded to other TPMG sites when solutions “prove their value,” and could include additional strategic support as a partner tech giant looks to advance their offering beyond TPMG.

Permanentech prepares to add more portfolio companies and partnerships “in the coming months,” according to its announcement.

According to recent reports, “For decades, our physicians have delivered high-quality, preventive care inside an integrated system where clinical expertise, data, and incentives all point toward keeping people healthy,” Maria Ansari, M.D., CEO and executive director of TPMG, noted. “Permanentech is our commitment to putting that ecosystem to work alongside the best technology from inside and outside our walls.”.

In a recent development, pleasanton, California-based TPMG is the country’s largest medical group, caring for 4.7 million Northern California members with about 10,000 physicians as well as nearly 47,000 nurses and support staff. It operates at 203 medical offices and facilities as well as 21 hospitals.

Recent findings suggest that its parent organization, Kaiser Permanente, is the country’s largest nonprofit health system by operating revenue ($127.7 billion in 2025). Topline financial results shared earlier this month outlined a 9% year-over-year increase in Q3 operating revenue, while the system’s Risant Health value-based care platform subsidiary in October announced prepares to acquire Integris Health, Oklahoma’s largest nonprofit provider.

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's aims to combine have earned the blessing of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a key hurdle that paves the path for a Jan. 1, 2027 close.

In a recent development, the nonprofit systems and the attorney general's office declared Monday an oversight agreement replete with service line preservation requirements and $2.15 billion of promised capital investments. Their deal is set to create a 39-hospital cross-regional health system that would be a major player in Minnesota's increasingly concentrated healthcare market.

According to recent reports, "My office has extensive authority to review healthcare transactions in Minnesota: we take it very seriously and with every review, we apply the lens of whether it will help you afford your life and live with dignity, safety and respect," Ellison stated in the announcement. "At the end of our thorough review of the transaction between Sutter and Allina, I have determined it passes the public-interest test.”.

According to recent reports, per the attorney general's office, the $2.5 billion be invested over five years to increase healthcare capacity in the state. That includes $150 million toward rural care, $50 million in workforce development and the scaling of virtual addiction therapy programs across the state.

The systems also agreed to maintain core services at rural locations for five years, to maintain reproductive and gender care for five years (as it complies with state and federal statute) and to continue Medicare participation and charity care. For Allina's workforce, they also agreed to retain all employees in good standing, honor all collective bargaining agreements and not enforce some noncompete agreements.

Ellison's office will enforce the five-year commitments via a 10-year period of oversight, which will include annual compliance reports from Sutter and Allina.

"In the context where the provision of healthcare everywhere is under serious financial strain and Allina is facing its own struggles, I appreciate that Sutter is entering Minnesota with a mindset of growth and an understanding that we cannot simply cut our way out of financial challenges and maintain Minnesota’s high standard of healthcare," Ellison said. "Sutter’s leadership has a history of delivering on growth and innovation and I look forward to their doing the same here.".

Since the nonprofits announced their deal back in March, Minnesota and the Midwest have been the stage for substantial health system dealmaking. Sanford Health announced and closed its acquisition of North Memorial Health, while Essentia Health and HealthPartners in September shared new prepares to combine and form an integrated 22-hospital organization.

According to recent reports, sutter and Allina, in a joint statement, thanked Ellison's office for the sign-off and remarked they proposal to close their transaction on Jan. 1, 2027.

"From the beginning, our vision has been grounded in a simple yet powerful belief: people across Minnesota and western Wisconsin deserve a sustainable health system that provides access to high-quality, affordable health care when and where they need it," the statement reads. "With our combined capabilities and more than $2 billion in investment, we will expand access to care, improve affordability, enhance care team and patient experiences and accelerate high-impact research and innovation.".

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's pending combination took a step forward this week with the signing of a definitive agreement, the nonprofit systems announced Thursday.

The agreement locks in the looks shared earlier this year in a letter of intent—namely, that the cross-market deal would bring more than $2 billion of investment to Allina's markets and that the smaller system would become the "Upper Midwest Division of Sutter Health.".

Now the organizations are left with securing state and federal regulatory approvals before the deal can close, which they expect to happen before the end of this year.

Recent findings suggest that “This crucial milestone brings us one step closer to our goal of partnering to enhance care, support our teams and expand clinical capabilities and research as a strong, nonprofit health system,” Lisa Shannon, president and CEO of Allina Health, said in Thursday's announcement. “With our combined expertise, complementary strengths and aligned missions and visions, I am confident we will be well-positioned to meet the evolving needs of our patients and communities now and well into the future.

Should the deal close, the resulting organization would span 39 hospitals as well as more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The organization would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health unveiled plans to join and form a 39-hospital, $26 billion nonprofit health system.

The pair mentioned Tuesday that they have signed a letter of intent for Allina to join Sutter. Allina would maintain its brand and regional headquarters but operate as the Upper Midwest Division of Sutter. Under that arrangement, Sutter is also committing $2 billion to bolster care access and patient experience investments in Allina’s Minnesota and western Wisconsin markets.

“This includes establishing new ambulatory and specialty care sites to fill care gaps and meet growing community needs, as well as recruiting more physicians and enhancing AI and digital health capabilities,” Sutter Health President and CEO Warner Thomas, who would maintain those titles should the deal close, stated in the announcement. “Building on our complementary strengths and combined expertise, we will build a healthcare innovation engine that accelerates how ideas move from development and design into improving the health of patients and communities.”.

Sources indicate that the systems said they plan to complete due diligence and finalize terms for a definitive agreement “over the coming weeks and months,” targeting a close before the end of 2026 should regulatory reviews run smoothly. A representative for Allina described the structure of the proposed agreement as being similar to a member substitution but noted that the deal's final structure will be outlined in the pending definitive agreement.

Industry observers note that alongside the 39 hospitals, the resulting organization would include more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The combination would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Among the benefits of their proposed partnership, the systems led their announcement with the synergistic technical expertise of their organizations and surrounding communities: Sutter’s immersion in Northern California's artificial intelligence and platform development and Allina’s seat in the medtech and engineering hub of Minnesota.

“The proposed combined system will be uniquely positioned to be a national leader in digital and technological advancements that meaningfully improve patients’ and caregivers’ experiences, while continuing to provide the compassionate care their respective communities have relied on for decades,” the announcement reads.

Such efforts, outlined in the announcement, include AI and digital solutions that would reduce administrative burdens for caregivers along with more convenient appointment scheduling for patients via digital consumer tools.

More broadly, the organizations said they expect the combination will help the organizations bolster physician and clinician recruitment, improve patient affordability and grow their capabilities, “particularly in clinical centers of excellence.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We are incredibly excited for the opportunity to harness the collective strength of our two mission-driven organizations to make a difference in the lives of our patients, communities and care teams,” mentioned Allina Health President and CEO Lisa Shannon, who would also maintain those titles in regard to the to-be-formed Upper Midwest Division. “As one nationally leading, locally committed nonprofit health system, we will be uniquely positioned to be at the forefront of innovation, building upon the expertise of our physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses and team members to chart a latest path for healthcare.”.

Twenty-seven-hospital Sutter is the larger of the two organizations, with $19.8 billion reported total revenue and a $509 million operating income in 2025 (excluding impacts of the to-be-approved 2025 Hospital Fee Program). In the past year, it opened 31 additional care sites, added more than 1,100 physicians and reached 3.6 million patients.

Allina reports $6 billion of revenue with a $95.4 million operating loss and has not had a positive operating margin for the past few years. It operates 12 hospitals and more than 100 other sites.

Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
